bullets: The new agent-benchmarks-clean release packages coding-agent tasks as immutable Linux containers with pinned configurations and SHA-256-verified layers. Its companion evaluation package fixes task subsets, harness versions, and scoring methods across Terminal Bench, software-engineering, and code-review evaluations. This is a new reproducibility artifact rather than a leaderboard update. [E001, E036] Why it matters: If you compare coding agents across machines or over time, this package lets you hold the execution environment and evaluator constant. That makes it easier to attribute score changes to the agent instead of changed dependencies, container contents, or harness versions. [E001, E036] Evidence: E001, E036. High confidence.

The new PIPETTE release evaluates prompt-injection attacks by whether they produce useful defenses, not only by attack success rate. Its source-authored description reports that a high attack success rate during automated red-teaming does not necessarily translate into stronger agents after adversarial training. [E009] Why it matters: If you are selecting an automated red-teaming method for tool-using agents, attack success alone is an incomplete selection metric. PIPETTE makes downstream robustness gains a separate evaluation target, connecting offensive testing to the defensive outcome the test is meant to improve. [E009] Evidence: E009. High confidence.

The new STEMBench release scores 12 postdoctoral-level problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics, and neuroscience using each field’s own measure of solution quality. Every problem also includes a no-domain-knowledge anchor and an expert anchor, rather than relying on answer matching or generic judging. [E017] Why it matters: If you are evaluating research agents, this design tests whether their work improves the quantity scientists actually optimize, not merely whether they reproduce a known answer. The anchors also provide interpretable reference points when raw scores differ across scientific fields. [E017] Evidence: E017. High confidence.

The new VideoACE benchmark tests whether a video agent uses interaction opportunities to improve understanding. It contains 1,000 questions over high-frame-rate action videos, where brief changes reward targeted observation, and supplies temporal evidence annotations and screened user hints. [E010] Why it matters: If you are choosing a suite for interactive video systems, VideoACE separates active evidence gathering from passive video question answering. That distinction matters for products whose models can seek additional frames or revisit specific moments before answering. [E010] Evidence: E010. High confidence.

Two new releases in the captured feed independently audit train-test leakage in scientific image and sequence benchmarks. The protein study replaces random splits with identity-controlled splits that keep related sequences together, while the BRISC brain-tumor audit reports exact and near-duplicate images crossing the official split. [E052, E077] Why it matters: If you evaluate models on biological sequences or medical images, random record-level splits may measure recognition of related or duplicated examples rather than generalization. These releases support making relationship-aware splitting and duplicate checks part of benchmark acceptance before comparing model rankings. [E052, E077] Evidence: E052, E077. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新版 agent-benchmarks-clean 将编码智能体任务封装为不可变的 Linux 容器，并采用固定配置和经 SHA-256 验证的层。其配套评估包为 Terminal Bench、软件工程和代码审查评估固定了任务子集、测试框架版本和评分方法。这是一个新的可复现性产物，而非排行榜更新。[E001, E036] Why it matters: 如果你要跨机器或跨时间比较编码智能体，该软件包可让执行环境和评估器保持不变，从而更容易将分数变化归因于智能体，而不是依赖项、容器内容或测试框架版本的变化。[E001, E036] Evidence: E001, E036. High confidence.

新版 PIPETTE 不仅依据攻击成功率，还依据提示注入攻击能否促成有效防御来进行评估。其由来源方撰写的说明指出，自动化红队测试中的高攻击成功率，并不一定会转化为对抗训练后更强的智能体。[E009] Why it matters: 如果你正在为工具调用型智能体选择自动化红队测试方法，仅看攻击成功率并不足以做出选择。PIPETTE 将下游鲁棒性提升设为独立的评估目标，把进攻性测试与该测试旨在改善的防御结果联系起来。[E009] Evidence: E009. High confidence.

新版 STEMBench 使用各领域自身的解答质量衡量标准，对高能物理学、天体物理学和神经科学中的 12 道博士后水平问题进行评分。每道题还包含一个无需领域知识的锚点和一个专家锚点，而非依赖答案匹配或通用评判。[E017] Why it matters: 如果你正在评估科研智能体，这一设计可检验其工作是否改善了科学家实际优化的量，而不只是能否复现已知答案。当不同科学领域的原始分数存在差异时，这些锚点也能提供可解释的参照点。[E017] Evidence: E017. High confidence.

新版 VideoACE 基准测试用于检验视频智能体是否会利用交互机会来增进理解。它包含针对高帧率动作视频的 1,000 个问题；视频中的短暂变化会使定向观察获得回报，并提供时间证据标注和经过筛选的用户提示。[E010] Why it matters: 如果你正在为交互式视频系统选择评测套件，VideoACE 可将主动收集证据与被动视频问答区分开来。对于模型能够在回答前主动获取更多帧或回看特定时刻的产品而言，这一区分非常重要。[E010] Evidence: E010. High confidence.

收录信息流中的两项新发布成果分别审计了科学图像和序列基准中的训练集—测试集泄漏。蛋白质研究用身份受控划分取代随机划分，将相关序列归在一起；BRISC 脑肿瘤审计则报告称，完全重复和近似重复的图像跨越了官方数据划分。[E052, E077] Why it matters: 如果你评估的是生物序列或医学图像模型，随机的记录级划分所衡量的可能是对相关或重复样本的识别，而非泛化能力。这些发布成果支持在比较模型排名之前，将关系感知的数据划分和重复项检查纳入基准验收流程。[E052, E077] Evidence: E052, E077. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.
evidence_items.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning

evidence_items.summary: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.
evidence_items.title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: Research-evaluation indicators are increasingly produced by large language models rather than human coders, yet the repeatability of machine annotation and the effect of rater disagreement on scores and rankings are rarely quantified. This paper examines both in two separate studies. In Study 1, a single LLM annotator coded 92 papers from three AI venues on the eleven rubric indicators of the 23-indicator Artificial Intelligence Meta-Science Index (AIMSI), producing 1,012 evidence-linked decisions that have not been verified by human coders. Same-model repeat coding of 15 papers gave pooled ordinal Krippendorff's alpha = .87 but drifted upward by 0.115 scale points; this measures consistency, not accuracy. Treating structurally inapplicable indicators as zero inflated the paper-type effect from epsilon-squared = .054 to .227, and the AIMSI–citation association fell from rho = .303 to .047 once venue and paper type were controlled. Study 2 is an external benchmark, not a validation of AIMSI: in a public dataset of 150 STEM-tutoring responses rated by three experts and judged by six LLM families, six-model consensus tracked the expert factuality ordering (Spearman rho = .748) but binary error agreement was moderate (Cohen's kappa = .386), against expert–expert kappa of .23–.83; 71.9% of items kept their tercile while the median item moved nine rank positions. Two lessons follow for composite indicators: score construct-inapplicable indicators as missing rather than zero, and report rank intervals, benchmarking judge–human agreement against measured expert–expert agreement. The suggestion that machine judges suit triage rather than exact ranking rests on Study 2 alone and remains a hypothesis for research evaluation until same-task human validation is done.
evidence_items.title: Machine-Assisted AI Research Evaluation Under Uncertainty: Study 2 external human–LLM agreement benchmark (analysis code and results)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This document describes the KnowAir-V2 dataset, a high-quality, large-scale data resource first introduced in our paper, "PCDCNet: A Surrogate Model for Air Quality Forecasting with Physical-Chemical Dynamics and Constraints"(arXiv:2505.19842). This dataset is specifically designed to serve as a benchmark for the development and validation of deep learning surrogate models that incorporate physical-chemical principles. Given that traditional numerical models are computationally expensive and pure data-driven models often lack physical consistency, this dataset aims to bridge that gap. The data has been preprocessed, including the imputation of missing values, and has been utilized in operational online forecasting systems. It serves as a robust foundation for building and evaluating interpretable, physically-consistent AI models for environmental science. Dataset Description Geographic and Temporal Coverage Regions: The dataset covers two major, densely populated regions in China: The Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and Surrounding Areas (BTHSA), with data from 228 monitoring stations. The Yangtze River Delta (YRD), with data from 127 monitoring stations. Temporal Span: The data spans from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2023, providing an extensive timeline for training and evaluation. A continuously updated extension continues the same stations from January 1, 2024 onward (currently to October 31, 2026); see Extension from 2024 below. All times are UTC.
evidence_items.title: KnowAir-V2: A Benchmark Dataset for Air Quality Forecasting with PCDCNet

evidence_items.summary: Systems for Natural Language to Visualization (NL2VIS) allow non-expert users to automatically perform exploratory visual analytics over complex multi-table databases. However, current Large Language Model (LLM) single-turn architectures have limitations including visual hallucinations, suboptimal perceptual channel selection, and failures on ambiguous or multi-table join queries. In this paper, we propose AgentViz, an autonomous multi-agent collaborative framework for hallucination-reduced, perceptually optimized data visualization. The architecture decomposes the visualization pipeline into four cooperating agents: (1) a Data Profiler Agent that extracts statistical moments, semantic column data types, and correlation topologies; (2) a Semantic Disambiguation and Hypothesis Agent that identifies analytical hypotheses and resolves semantic constraints; (3) a Perceptual Visual Design Agent that leverages Cleveland-McGill graphical perception rankings to generate declarative Vega-Lite specifications; and (4) a Quality Critic and Verification Agent that performs closed-loop verification to identify field hallucinations and visual distortions. Evaluated on 25,750 natural language queries across 105 domains in the nvBench 2.0 benchmark, AgentViz reports an overall Visualization Exact Match Accuracy of 93.65%, a 10-fold reduction in visual hallucinations (1.15% versus 11.80%), and 89.20% accuracy on ambiguous multi-table queries, with an inference latency of 1.14 seconds per visualization. The framework aims to provide a verifiable approach to automated visual analytics and AI-assisted data visualization.
evidence_items.title: AgentViz: An Autonomous Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for Hallucination-Free Natural Language Data Visualization on the nvBench Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
evidence_items.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.
evidence_items.title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions

evidence_items.summary: Video rough-cut is a core stage in media production workflows, organizing raw media materials into an initial video cut. Despite recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) for video-related tasks, automatic rough-cut remains underexplored, without a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation or mature workflows for producing executable cut plans. To address the evaluation gap, we introduce RoughCut-Bench, which covers two practical settings: (1) a visually driven setting over video cases, covering highlight detection and selection, source-video ordering, and adherence to user requirements when provided; and (2) a speech-driven setting over automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, covering filler removal, expression deduplication, and low-value content trimming. Across these settings, the benchmark contains 101 visually driven cases, including 831 raw videos with 1,476 highlight annotations. It also includes 84 speech-driven cases, each consisting of an ASR transcript with annotated cleanup spans. The evaluation compares cut plans with these annotations in both settings and additionally uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator to assess rendered-cut quality in the visual setting. To apply LVLMs to automatic rough-cut, we further propose agentic workflows that guide them to produce structured cut plans from input materials. Experiments show that current LVLMs remain limited in producing expert-aligned cut plans. Our benchmark, code, and prompts are released at https://whalesong-zrs.github.io/RoughCut-Bench-Project-Page.
evidence_items.title: RoughCut-Bench: A Benchmark for Automatic Video Rough-Cut with Large Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Background: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a morbid but underrecognized disease diagnosed by right heart catheterization (RHC). Automated extraction of RHC data from electronic health systems is likely to expedite PH diagnosis. However, RHC outputs are typically unstructured, free-text reports and current large language models (LLM) that extract patient-level RHC data are imprecise and derived from small datasets. Methods and Results: We established an iterative development and validation framework using the LLM GPT-4-0125-preview to extract patient-level data from RHC reports. The extraction accuracy was assessed against manual expert-curated ground truth using micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 metrics across all extracted variables. Evaluation on an independent test set of 100 previously unseen reports yielded a precision of 99.8%, a recall of 99.5%, an F1 score of 99.8%, and a hallucination rate of 0.09%. Next, we deployed the LLM to all n = 17,151 RHC reports captured in the Electronic Health Record of the University of Maryland Medical System (UMMS; ~2.3 million patients across 12 hospitals) from 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2024. Manual validation on 200 random reports demonstrated a precision of 99.7%, a recall of 99.2%, an F1 score of 99.5%, and a hallucination rate of 0.17% (all realistic and physiologically plausible). To further explore reproducibility across deployment settings, we deployed the LLM to a targeted sample of 3000 randomly selected RHC reports that included previously identified error cases. Validation of 200 random reports demonstrated a hallucination rate of 0.33% (precision 99.4%, recall 99.9%, F1 99.6%). Notably, four of the seven observed hallucinations in the large-scale deployment were absent when processed in a smaller deployment cohort. Conclusions: We demonstrate high precision for LLMs when deployed on a scale to RHC reports from a large, diverse multi-hospital EHR.
evidence_items.title: Large-Scale Deployment of Large Language Models to Extract Hemodynamic Variables from Cardiac Catheterization

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background : Patient-level clinico-transcriptomic cohorts are used for biomarker discovery, patient stratification, validation and model training. However, most transcriptomic data remains siloed in hospitals, biopharma, and consortia because expression profiles and linked clinical metadata carry re-identification risk. Synthetic RNA-seq cohorts that capture population structure without retaining individual records could be shared in their place, but only if they accurately reproduce the results of standard translational analyses on the real data. We test this with dbTwin, a proprietary generator, on three public cohorts, so that every synthetic result can be checked against its real source, and release the synthetic cohorts with the benchmark used to evaluate them. Results: Synthetic versions of TCGA lung adenocarcinoma (510 samples; 19,719 genes), whole-blood sepsis (152; 27,097), and pediatric inflammatory bowel disease (322; 43,790) recovered most of the differential-expression (DE) signals tested. Across five contrasts on clinical variables declared to dbTwin as anchor columns, synthetic effect sizes kept their real magnitude (log2 fold-change slope 0.92–1.01), and 71.9–90.8% of real DE genes were recovered (81.7–97.2% at a relaxed screening threshold). For STK11 mutation (non-anchor column), effect sizes shrank (slope 0.70) but 96.8% of DE genes kept their direction. In five-fold cross-validation, classifiers trained on synthetic data were within 0.002 ROC-AUC of real-trained ones on held-out real patients and relied on largely the same driver genes (SHAP Pearson r = 0.808–0.975). Synthetic cohorts also retained gene–gene co-expression (Spearman ρ = 0.940–0.996), and 0 of 22 clinical comparisons exceeded sampling noise.
evidence_items.title: Biomarker discovery on synthetic patient transcriptomes: three public cohorts and a benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present MitoEM 2.0, a difficulty-aware extension of the original MitoEM benchmark for training and evaluating three-dimensional (3D) mitochondria instance segmentation in volume electron microscopy. The collection assembles multiscale vEM datasets (FIB-SEM, SBF-SEM, ssSEM) spanning diverse tissues and species, with expert-verified instance labels emphasizing biologically difficult scenarios, including dense mitochondrial packing, hyperfused networks, and thin filamentous connections with ambiguous boundaries. All releases include native-resolution volumes and standardized processed versions, per-volume metadata (voxel size, modality, tissue, splits), and official train/validation/test partitions to enable reproducible benchmarking. Annotations follow a consistent protocol with quality checks and instance reindexing. Data are provided in NIfTI with nnU-Net–compatible layout and OME-Zarr for cloud-aware workflows, alongside machine-readable split files and checksums. Baseline scripts support common training pipelines and size-stratified evaluation. By consolidating challenging volumes and harmonized labels, MitoEM 2.0 facilitates robust model development and fair comparison across methods while supporting reuse in bioimage analysis, algorithm benchmarking, and teaching.
evidence_items.title: MitoEM 2.0: A Benchmark for Challenging 3D Mitochondria Instance Segmentation from EM Images

evidence_items.summary: Collaborative learning scripts are usually fixed, and collaboration dashboards do not necessarily prompt teachers to intervene. We present a hybrid intelligent decision-support architecture that diagnoses five group dysfunctions, explains each alert and proposes one script adaptation from a closed catalogue, with an open simulation benchmark providing planted dysfunctions and a per-group oracle. It combines fuzzy inference, a lexical content classifier, calibrated gradient-boosting detectors with SHAP explanations, expected-benefit operator selection and NSGA-II regrouping. All evidence comes from controlled simulations; no teacher used the system, and learning outcomes were not evaluated. Over 20 development datasets, the detectors reached a macro-F1 of 0.591, and the fuzzy indicators were practically equivalent to their absence in accuracy. Because development data, including test windows of one seed, were inspected while the system was built, these results are not an independent confirmation; a pre-specified evaluation of the frozen system on 20 new datasets replicated 14 of 15 endpoints (macro-F1 0.590), but the defect rate of filtered explanations doubled (0.029 to 0.059). Performance did not survive distribution shift: macro-F1 fell from 0.586 to 0.297 under a changed generating mechanism, the full model fell below the interaction-only model on a held-out topic, and misconception F1 on unseen paraphrases (0.146) was no better than flagging every window. A training-selected operating point achieved 0.399 of the oracle’s simulated harm reduction with 18.7% unneeded interventions, and detector-triggered regrouping increased simulated harm. The benchmark serves as a pre-deployment stress test; the scores are upper bounds, not evidence of teaching benefit.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Intelligent Decision-Support Architecture for Explainable Adaptation of Collaborative Learning Scripts: A Simulation Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract While spatial transcriptomics technologies are increasingly accessible, spatial proteomics remains constrained by high costs and limited throughput. Furthermore, poor mRNA-protein correlation, driven by post-transcriptional regulation, necessitates multi-omics integration for complementary biological insights. Current RNA-to-protein prediction models, primarily trained on bulk or single-cell data, often overlook critical spatial context. Consequently, it remains unclear which model architecture, spatial representation, or histopathological features best facilitate spatial protein abundance inference. To address these gaps, we defined the STP (Spatial Transcriptome-to-Proteome) task and launched the STP Open Challenge, a competition for predicting spatial proteomics from spatial transcriptomics of adjacent tissue sections. Utilizing a curated paired spatial dataset and a standardized evaluation framework, the challenge attracted 101 teams and yielded 896 valid submissions. Top-performing methods achieved strong predictive performance while preserving spatial organization. The landscape of submitted models revealed diverse modeling strategies and motivated us to develop a consensus-based ensemble framework that leverages various participant methods to enhance prediction robustness. Extended evaluation on unseen datasets demonstrated that the top-performing models outperformed existing baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of the community effort for this task. By formally defining the STP task and providing a standardized benchmarking platform, this work establishes a foundation for scalable, cost-effective spatial proteomics prediction and future multi-omics integration.
evidence_items.title: The STP Open Challenge: A Community Effort to Define and Benchmark Spatial Transcriptome-to-Proteome Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems

evidence_items.summary: Agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous tasks, yet existing evaluations mostly focus on task success rather than whether agents know when to abstain. This gap poses real risks: under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures, agents may execute unintended and irreversible actions. To close this gap, we present the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention: the calibrated ability of tool-using LLM agents to recognize when not to act. At its core, AgentAbstain is a paired-task benchmark built on an agent-native taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios across pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery. It contains 263 paired tasks across 42 executable sandbox environments, where each pair consists of a should-act task and a should-abstain variant produced through a controlled perturbation to the instruction, tool, or environment state. To scale this paired design and resist data contamination, we propose AbstainGen, a fully automated pipeline that synthesizes sandbox environments and generates paired tasks end-to-end, validated by deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges; fresh task instances can be regenerated on demand, and three independent annotators rate 94-98% of sampled tasks as well-designed. Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 agent harnesses, the best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy (correct on both the act and abstain sides of each paired task). More importantly, abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability, indicating that scaling task-solving alone will not close this gap. We further identify failure modes such as post-hoc abstention, in which agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers. Our code and dataset are open-sourced at agentabstain.github.io.
evidence_items.title: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?

evidence_items.summary: The RISE Humanities Data Benchmark, maintained by RISE (Research and Infrastructure Support) at the University of Basel, evaluates large language models on tasks from humanities research: transcribing, interpreting and extracting structured data from historical documents such as letters, library cards, newspaper advertisements and medieval manuscripts, scored against ground truths defined by domain experts, with the cost and runtime of every request. Every stored result of the Humanities Data Benchmark as joinable tables: 3,861 runs, 168,916 requests and 3,970,787 metric observations covering data through 2026-11-18. Apart from the framework's own test benchmarks, nothing is filtered: unscored, failed and unresolved runs are rows carrying a status rather than omissions. Tables in Parquet, a metric dictionary, coverage, diagnostics and a source manifest, with the original request and scoring JSON as gzipped JSON Lines. A new release follows each release of the benchmark software; each is a complete snapshot. README.md documents the tables and how to use them, CHANGELOG.md what changed between releases.

evidence_items.summary: Overhead aerial imagery feeds dense-prediction pipelines that are routinely trained in one geographic region and deployed in another, yet no benchmark measures how shadow detection models transfer across regions. Existing overhead shadow datasets either lack a geographic transfer protocol or rely on automatically generated labels. We introduce ShadowTransfer, a benchmark of 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities at two native resolutions, paired with a leave-one-city-out evaluation protocol. Under vanilla training, holding out the test city costs 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU across four architectures, the gap remains significant when the training set grows from 225 to 900 images, and six of eight adaptation methods degrade more than vanilla training on average. We propose a three-probe framework that diagnoses where and how the transfer breaks: the failure operates in feature space, beyond the reach of pixel-histogram matching, shows up as a confidence collapse on shadow pixels while background confidence stays intact, and is recoverable by retraining different architectural components depending on the model: encoder for some, decoder for others. These findings replicate on INRIA building footprints, suggesting they describe geographic transfer beyond shadows. Guided by the diagnosis, we build Spectral Information Bottleneck (SIB), a plug-in module with one component per finding. Across the 9 (architecture, held-out city) cells, SIB has the smallest mean gap to the within-city upper bound of the ten methods we evaluate (6.42 mIoU), level with FDA. The benchmark, LOCO protocol, code, and trained models are released to support reproducible evaluation of geographic transfer in overhead dense prediction.
evidence_items.title: ShadowTransfer: A Geographic Transfer Benchmark for Overhead Shadow Detection

evidence_items.summary: Embodied AI systems, such as drones and autonomous vehicles, improve navigation by enhancing perception in environments containing unseen objects. While Visual Language Models (VLMs) offer strong image understanding, their real-world application is underexplored. For effective deployment, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models, leveraging models like CLIP to assign pixel-level labels from text, must be robust to outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and varying viewpoints. Despite their potential, these models encounter significant challenges in cross-domain generalization, hindering their practical use in embodied AI applications. In this work, we present Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary segmentation across both aerial and ground perspectives. This benchmark supports thorough evaluation across different viewpoints and sensor modalities. We assess foundational models like CLIP and advanced OVSS models using a curated dataset that spans varied outdoor conditions, sim-to-real scenarios, and multiple sensors, including infrared, to support the development of robust and generalizable perception systems. We also present a novel framework, Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ), which jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across RGB and infrared imagery. This approach supports robust evaluation of open-vocabulary segmentation models across diverse environmental conditions. Our work sets a robustness-driven benchmark, providing key insights and laying the foundation for future research in open-world embodied AI perception. The benchmark and project page are available at https://aniruddhsikdar1.github.io/publications/pixel2perspective/
evidence_items.title: Pixel2Perspective: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal and Multi-View Generalization in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: E-commerce visual effects (EVF) are dynamic, product-centered visual presentations in e-commerce videos, often accompanied by promotional text. They play an important role in attracting viewer attention and conveying product information. However, general measures of visual quality and text relevance alone do not establish whether generated videos preserve product appearance, maintain readable text, and produce coherent, contextually appropriate effects. To address this issue, we introduce EVF-Bench, a dedicated benchmark spanning six evaluation dimensions: visual quality and text relevance as general dimensions, and motion, product consistency, text stability, and creative rationality as EVF-specific dimensions. To complement the benchmark and support task-aligned research and model adaptation, we further construct EVF-32K, a dataset of over 32000 curated image-text-video triples tailored to e-commerce scenarios. Using this suite, we systematically evaluate representative video generation models and their domain-adapted variants. The results reveal complementary strengths, with no evaluated configuration leading all six dimensions. Together, EVF-Bench and EVF-32K provide a task-oriented evaluation framework and a supporting data resource for e-commerce video generation.
evidence_items.title: EVF-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for E-commerce Visual Effects in Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.
evidence_items.title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises

evidence_items.summary: Composite image restoration aims to recover images corrupted by multiple coexisting degradations. Existing methods predominantly decompose composite corruptions into individual factors, relying on these isolated priors to guide restoration. However, coexisting degradations are inherently interdependent: the manifestation of one degradation dynamically shifts with the states of others, inducing non-additive interactions that factor-wise paradigms fail to capture. To bridge this gap, we formulate state-dependent cross-degradation responses and propose PROBE, an interventional framework that explicitly models how coexisting degradations influence one another. Specifically, we first construct unified degradation axes by aligning visual and textual degraded-clean offsets. Along these axes, a calibrated coordinate head estimates current degradation states, while bidirectional feature perturbations are injected to probe cross-coordinate responses under the current states. Contrasting these responses with corresponding intensity-matched single-degradation references quantifies intrinsic non-additive deviations, allowing the resulting response descriptors and state coordinates to jointly guide restoration. For comprehensive evaluation, we introduce SCD-15, a new benchmark covering all 15 nonempty combinations of four degradation factors at three severity levels. Experiments demonstrate that PROBE achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CDD-11, AWMM-100K, and SCD-15 composite restoration datasets using a compact model with modest GPU memory requirements.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Additive Composition: Interventional Modeling of State-Dependent Cross-Degradation Responses for Composite Image Restoration

evidence_items.summary: Put a monocular mesh estimator behind every camera of a calibrated rig, and the reconstructed bodies land a meter or more apart. The cause is geometric: each estimate sits at the depth implied by a focal length the network assumed, not the one the camera has. Its error therefore points almost entirely along its own viewing ray, and the calibration tells us that direction exactly. To address this, we introduce the Ray-Lateral Agreement (RLA), which follows one rule: trust the ray, not the depth. RLA first slides every estimate along its own rays, which removes the depth bias and leaves the shape untouched. It then fuses the views one point at a time, under a Gaussian error whose precision follows each viewing ray. The maximum-likelihood solution is closed-form, interpolates between averaging and midpoint triangulation, and stays well conditioned where triangulation is singular. Robustness is the harder half, because correct views also disagree along their rays. Any weight built on the full residual therefore punishes good views together with bad ones. Ray-lateral agreement instead scores every view, at every point, by its residual across that view's own ray alone. We evaluated RLA on multi-camera public benchmark datasets. Across two, three, and four cameras and three per-view pose estimators, RLA consistently achieves lower worst-case error than all triangulation baselines.
evidence_items.title: Trust the Ray, Not the Depth: Ray-Lateral Agreement for Multi-View 3D Human Pose Fusion

evidence_items.summary: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.
evidence_items.title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.
evidence_items.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Causal discovery is increasingly applied to healthcare data, where the recovered relationships can encode biased pathways that propagate to downstream prediction. Path-specific fairness analysis, through direct, indirect, and spurious effect decompositions along with fairness-utility ratio assessment allows bias quantification and associated prediction cost. However, existing evaluations of causal discovery under fairness constraints have largely used non-clinical datasets and have not separated the contribution of confounders from that of mediators, leaving open how discovery-algorithm choice propagates through path-specific fairness to the utility trade-off in clinical settings. This work addresses that gap by establishing an expert-elicited causal graph benchmark for the heart failure clinical records dataset and tracing discovery algorithms through composite, per-variable fairness decompositions and fairness-utility ratio. ICA-LiNGAM achieves the lowest structural Hamming distance and highest recall, while GES achieves the highest precision. For path-specific effects, there was a 1.2 percentage-point difference in the mediated effect on ejection fraction on overall causal fairness between the original and discovered graphs. This ultimately led to variations in the fairness-utility ratio highlighting need for fine-grained evaluation. These results indicate that discovery-aware, path-specific fairness evaluation is consequential in clinical settings and warrants inclusion in routine auditing of clinical risk models.
evidence_items.title: Auditing Path-Specific Fairness Across Causal Discovery Algorithms: A Heart Failure Case Study

evidence_items.summary: A central challenge for multimodal language models (MLLMs) in real-world tasks is to abstract visual observations into structured spatial states and reason over how those states change under actions over long horizons. Existing multimodal benchmarks often focus on static question answering, where answers can be directly extracted from images, or assume symbolic states are available and bypass the visual-to-spatial abstraction process. We present MARBLE, a diagnostic benchmark for spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning across three agent environments: CUBE, MAZE, and BLOX. MARBLE spans 2D and 3D spatial puzzles under geometric constraints, dynamic layouts, and spatial transformations, with difficulty systematically controlled along two axes: observation format and planning horizon. Extensive evaluations show that frontier MLLMs struggle on MARBLE, with the strongest model GPT-5.4 achieving only a 7.3% average success rate across the three environments in the hardest setting. Pairwise ablations on the open-weight models identify visual-to-spatial abstraction as the major bottleneck: when models must infer spatial states from images instead of receiving human-annotated states, success drops from 50.7% to 3.7% for Gemma-4-31B and from 87.9% to 6.5% for Kimi-K2.6. The results indicate that models often fail to construct precise spatial states from visual observations before planning, a task that is straightforward for humans. Overall, MARBLE reveals the gap in reliable visual-to-spatial abstraction for frontier MLLMs and provides a controlled testbed for measuring progress in spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning.
evidence_items.title: MARBLE: An Agentic Benchmark for Spatial Reasoning and Visual Abstraction

evidence_items.summary: Cell tracking in time-lapse microscopy is essential for studying dynamic biological processes such as migration, proliferation, and lineage formation. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on high-framerate imaging, where short temporal intervals simplify correspondence between cells across consecutive frames. We present the Low Frame-rate Cell Tracking dataset (LFCT), a benchmark dataset designed specifically for evaluating cell tracking methods under low-frame-rate conditions. The dataset contains multi-day live-cell microscopy sequences from four human cell lines (MCF10A, MDA-MB-231, HEK293T, and U87), acquired at 10× and 20× magnifications using phase-contrast and fluorescence imaging (nucleus). Ground-truth annotations include cell identifications, temporal linking, lineage relationships, and mitosis events. To generate reliable annotations, automated segmentation and tracking were combined with extensive manual curation. LFCT provides a comprehensive resource for developing and benchmarking robust cell tracking algorithms capable of handling sparse temporal sampling and large inter-frame motion in long-term live-cell imaging experiments.

evidence_items.summary: RevertBench: Synthetic Evidence-Update Benchmark and LLM Reliability Audit Data RevertBench is a synthetic benchmark designed to evaluate the reliability of small language models when previously supplied evidence is withdrawn, reinstated, or changed. It investigates whether language models can produce correct final decisions while accurately tracking and reporting the evidence available at each stage. The repository contains 2,108 archived model responses collected across multiple experimental conditions. These responses represent repeated evaluations and different model configurations rather than 2,108 independent benchmark cases. The benchmark uses a deterministic Boolean oracle to establish ground-truth decisions. Evaluation focuses on four aspects of model reliability: final decision accuracy (ALLOW/DENY), correctness of reported active evidence records, validity of structured JSON responses, and logical consistency between the reported evidence state and final decision. The repository includes synthetic benchmark cases, frozen evaluation plans, archived model responses, experimental metadata, supplementary analyses, reproducibility scripts, verification notebooks, and file-integrity checksums. These materials support independent verification of the reported results without requiring additional model training or inference. The experiments examine several small language-model checkpoints under controlled evidence-update scenarios. Additional analyses investigate the effects of model selection, prompt constraints, structured-output requirements, and variations in evidence complexity. Limitations: RevertBench uses simplified synthetic scenarios rather than real-world operational documents. Some evaluation choices were informed by preliminary experiments, and the models tested represent a limited set of architectures and configurations.
evidence_items.title: RevertBench: Synthetic Evidence-Update Benchmark and LLM Reliability Audit Data

evidence_items.summary: Applying natural language processing-related algorithms is currently a popular project in legal applications, for instance, document classification of legal documents, contract review and machine translation. Using the above machine learning algorithms, all need to encode the words in the document in the form of vectors. The word embedding model is a modern distributed word representation approach and the most common unsupervised word encoding method. It facilitates subjecting other algorithms and subsequently performing the downstream tasks of natural language processing vis-à-vis. The most common and practical approach of accuracy evaluation with the word embedding model uses a benchmark set with linguistic rules or the relationship between words to perform analogy reasoning via algebraic calculation. This paper proposes establishing a 1,256 Legal Analogical Reasoning Questions Set (LARQS) from the 2,388 Chinese Codex corpus using five kinds of legal relations, which are then used to evaluate the accuracy of the Chinese word embedding model. Moreover, we discovered that legal relations might be ubiquitous in the word embedding model.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Language models are revolutionizing the biochemistry domain, assisting scientists in drug design and chemical synthesis with high efficiency. Yet current approaches struggle between small language models prone to hallucination and limited knowledge retention, and large cloud-based language models plagued by privacy risks and high inference costs. To bridge this gap, we introduce ChemCRAFT, a novel framework leveraging agentic reinforcement learning to decouple chemical reasoning from knowledge storage. Instead of forcing the model to memorize vast chemical data, our approach empowers the language model to interact with a sandbox for precise information retrieval. This externalization of knowledge allows a locally deployable small model to achieve superior performance while being highly token-efficient compared to traditional multi-agent systems. To enable small language models for agent-calling ability, we build an agentic trajectory construction pipeline and a comprehensive chemical-agent sandbox. Based on sandbox interactions, we constructed ChemToolDataset, the first large-scale chemical tool trajectory dataset. Simultaneously, we propose SMILES-GRPO to build a dense chemical reward function, promoting the model's ability to call chemical agents. Evaluations across diverse aspects of drug design show that ChemCRAFT outperforms current cloud-based LLMs in molecular structure analysis, molecular optimization, and synthesis pathway prediction, demonstrating that scientific reasoning is not solely an emergent ability of model scale, but a learnable policy of tool orchestration. Furthermore, assessments in real-world drug optimization scenarios, including fentanyl analog optimization and pro-inflammatory GSTO1 inhibitors optimization, reveal that ChemCRAFT generates optimization trajectories mirroring human experts, confirming its reliability as a scientific assistant.
evidence_items.title: Agentic reinforcement learning empowers next-generation chemical language models for molecular design and synthesis

evidence_items.summary: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across \nvideos{} videos generated by \nmodels{} open models from $140$ start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to $7.3$ times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.
evidence_items.title: StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency in Interactive Video World Model

evidence_items.summary: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.
evidence_items.title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?

authors: Yiming Cheng, Chris Low, Binrui Huang, Mengshi Zhang, Zihao Chen, Kate Keahey, Paul Marshall, Kexin Pei
evidence_items.summary: AI agents are transforming scientific computing and software workflows, but generating and executing code requires a correctly configured execution environment. Automating environment construction remains difficult because repositories encode heterogeneous, often incomplete requirements for operating systems, toolchains, dependencies, and build procedures. Existing workflows thus rely on developer-maintained Dockerfiles and setup scripts, making preparation labor-intensive, hard to scale, and potentially biasing evaluations. We present ENVAGENT, an agentic framework that synthesizes, builds, and verifies repository-level Docker environments. ENVAGENT combines deterministic utilities for Docker execution and state management with coordinated agents for repository analysis, planning, Dockerfile synthesis, and iterative failure diagnosis and repair. We also introduce ENVBENCH, a benchmark of 54 scientific artifacts and open-source repositories spanning seven languages from Chameleon Trovi and Multi-SWE-bench. For each repository, we curate a declarative rubric of required structure, configuration, and functionality, and a shared evaluator applies 2,108 weighted checks across generated environments. Across four matched language-model settings, ENVAGENT constructs 43.5 executable environments out of 54 on average, versus 23.5 for Codex and Claude Code, and scores 62.02 versus 24.19 on a composite of executability and rubric satisfaction. These results show that environment-specific agent orchestration substantially improves automated environment construction.

evidence_items.summary: Misleading news often reaches readers before its claims can be checked, which has encouraged research into artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) as tools for flagging content that needs closer examination. This paper reviews 31 publications from 2011 to 2024 and organises their approaches into four groups: traditional machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based models, and multi-source or real-time systems. It then tests one concern that recurs in the literature, namely that scores measured on one dataset do not carry over to another. Four standard classifiers (Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, and Random Forest, all on TF-IDF features) were evaluated on two public datasets: Fake or Real News (2016 political articles) and CoAID (2020 COVID-19 articles). Within Fake or Real News, five-fold macro-F1 ranges from 0.87 to 0.94. When a model trained on one dataset is tested on the other, macro-F1 falls to between 0.06 and 0.42. A model trained on an early CoAID snapshot also detects few fake articles in later snapshots, although the later test set holds only 15 fake articles, so that result is inconclusive. The highest-weighted terms of the linear models include source and formatting words, which suggests dataset-specific shortcuts. The paper also specifies CAMMS, a multilingual and multimodal framework with an explanation layer. CAMMS is described and given an evaluation plan, but it has not been implemented or evaluated here. The review finds no basis for naming one model family as best in every setting, and it points to cross-dataset testing, multilingual evaluation, transparent reporting, and human oversight as priorities.
evidence_items.title: AI-Based Fake News Detection Using Natural Language Processing: A Review and Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.
evidence_items.title: Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability

evidence_items.summary: We introduce MANGO Arena, an open-source testbed in which four LLM agents each run one company in a serial supply chain adapted from MANGO, a classroom factory-management game. The environment enforces hard rules (a truck limit, a no-credit cash constraint and production capacity), logs every blocked attempt to break them, and gives agents a public message board on which side payments are explicitly forbidden. This lets one environment measure three things at once: an economic outcome (the bullwhip effect), rule adherence under pressure, and proposals to collude. In a pilot with three small reasoning models, two scripted reference policies, two conditions (with and without a supplier fire) and three demand seeds, all LLM agents amplified demand variability as it moved upstream, by 7 to 25 times at the Retailer and 13 to 179 times at the Supplier, often more than a textbook order-up-to policy. They did so largely by ordering in batches (zero orders in up to 60% of decisions). Real rule violations were rare (at most 7 of 288 decisions per model) and no agent proposed a money side deal. The pilot's main lesson concerns evaluation method. API failures (rate limits and runaway hidden reasoning) entered the metrics silently as "no order" decisions. And when we reran games with the same seeds and no failed calls, upstream bullwhip changed by up to 17 times between runs. With three seeds, conclusions about how a disruption affects a given model did not survive a rerun. We report these failures in full and propose reporting practices for multi-agent evaluations of this kind. Code, prompts and every logged decision are public.
evidence_items.title: MANGO Arena: Same Seeds, Different Chains Evaluating LLM Agents in a Disrupted Supply Chain

evidence_items.summary: Remote smartphone recommerce is scaling quickly, and locking a repurchase offer from seller photos and diagnostic screens before the handset arrives has become a central operational task. Existing multimodal resources mainly target defect localization, catalog attributes, or screen reading. They overlook payout-facing scorecards with dual cosmetic and operational ground truth under a declared input contract. This gap stems from two challenges: (1) the lack of a large weakly labeled trade-in corpus kept separate from a compact audited ranking cut, and (2) architectures that either flatten unordered photo bags into one prompt or collapse evaluation into a single price scalar. To address these challenges, we propose PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-ground-truth recommerce framework with PhoneValue-Corpus for weak training on 21,550 orders and 278,748 images, and PV-Rank as the only leaderboard on 335 quality-gated orders. Systems are ranked by CardScore under LeadGate, with Cosmetic Fill and Operational Fill as diagnostics, while grade and price stay off the board. Notably, ValueAgent is a six-stage perception-fusion reference that canonicalizes views, detects regional defects, reads screenshots, and fuses evidence under warehouse-style rules, so bag-of-images prompting is not the only evaluation unit. On the same PV-Rank cut and frozen scorer, this full-system and input-contract comparison finds ValueAgent at 84.1 CardScore against the strongest Flat Vision-Language Model at 69.9, with the largest reported gap in CosFill, while OpsFill remains limited under the two declared contracts. CardScore measures field-fill completeness, not quote accuracy.
evidence_items.title: PhoneValue-Bench: A Dual-Ground-Truth Scorecard Benchmark for Smartphone Recommerce Inspection

evidence_items.summary: ThermoNO-MPC v0.1.2 is a Python toolkit for reproducible comparison and diagnosis of predictive controllers for synthetic multi-zone thermal processes. This version makes same-plan replay and common-state comparison reusable library functions, adds a responsive linear thermal predictor with a complete CPU workflow, and reports unsupported neural time intervals and horizons before inference. The release also adds configurable SLSQP scaling/start settings and prediction-grid adapters. The original benchmark, six original checkpoints and historical D1-D11 evidence are preserved separately from the revision studies. Properly scaled SLSQP changes the restricted original controller ranking; the software does not claim universal neural or optimizer superiority. Files and use. The source snapshot, Python wheel and source distribution are accompanied by SHA-256 checksums. Start with README.md and REPRODUCE.md, then run the CPU examples, including examples/predictor workflow.py. A matching installed final wheel is checked in a fresh CPU environment without PyTorch. The Windows/Python 3.11.9 software suite contains 53 passing tests; numerical replay preserves the six original N03 neural traces, excluding elapsed times. Related computation. The complete version 0.1.2 computational record is available at 10.5281/zenodo.24019545 . It contains the training data, numeric weights, raw control/forecast records, executed-source snapshots, controlled revision studies and separate serial timing results. The computation archive distinguishes a saved-record CPU audit from a full experimental rerun. Source and history. Versioned source: GitHub v0.1.2 . Historical software: v0.1.1 ; historical computation: v0.1.1 computation . Scope and license. This is an uncalibrated synthetic research workflow, not an industrial validation or thermal safety guarantee. Predicted-plan rejection and PID fallback can still yield realized constraint violations.

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an economic study of a novel Thermal Energy Storage system, the Thermal Energy Storage and Exchange with Integrated Rotating Media Transport (T.E. Sandewirm, i.e. Sandewirm). The Sandewirm technology is a sensible energy storage device using solid particle media that is horizontally conveyed through an inner and outer annulus. This allows for a charging and discharging heat exchanger to reside within an endcap, where particles are moved between inner and outer annuli, eliminating the need for vertical conveyance systems that are necessary for two-tank systems. Sandewirm’s economic performance is evaluated in three potential applications—Gen3 concentrated solar power, long-duration energy storage, and industrial steam generation—through back-to-back levelized cost of storage (LCOS) comparison against incumbent TES technologies. An object-oriented Python cost analysis framework is constructed and facilitates the use of detailed and customized cost factors, Monte Carlo simulations, and financial models to most closely estimate each case’s LCOS. Results from this study show that the Sandewirm design is competitive with current state-of-the-art TES technologies for Gen3 concentrated solar power, long-duration energy storage, and solar steam generation cases, resulting in 7.7%, 4.2%, and 72% reduction in lifetime project costs, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark LCOS Analysis of the T.E. Sandewirm Technology

evidence_items.summary: This study investigates deep learning-based vehicle type classification from LiDAR point clouds in motorway traffic scenes. Using stationary, roadside LiDAR sensors, the work aims to distinguish vehicle categories such as motorcycles, passenger cars, vans, trucks, buses, and trailer combinations in a non-invasive, privacy-preserving, and weather-independent manner. In addition to model comparison, a major contribution of the work is the creation and validation of a project-specific LiDAR dataset, derived from an initial dimension-based CoMark pre-classification and subsequently verified through manual labeling. To assess the suitability of contemporary point cloud architectures, DGCNN with PAConv, PointNeXt, and Point Transformer V3 (PTv3) were trained on the manually validated dataset. The experimental results indicate that PointNeXt achieved the strongest overall performance, reaching 96.74% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.942, while also exhibiting the lowest model complexity among the best-performing methods. PTv3 attained similarly high classification accuracy but required substantially more parameters, whereas DGCNN with PAConv showed robust performance at the cost of significantly higher training effort. Class-wise analysis and confusion matrices reveal that the remaining errors occur primarily among structurally similar commercial vehicle classes, highlighting the geometric ambiguity inherent in the dataset. Overall, the findings demonstrate that deep learning on LiDAR point clouds offers a scalable and effective solution for vehicle classification in traffic monitoring applications, while careful dataset preparation, validation, and class-specific analysis remain crucial for robust real-world deployment. To support reproducibility, the dataset, data loader, and training instructions will be released in a public GitHub repository: https://github.com/xGeorg315/tls81-roadside-lidar-vehicle-classification.
evidence_items.title: A Real-World LiDAR Benchmark for Fine-Grained Vehicle Classification

evidence_items.summary: Protein functional-class classifiers are usually evaluated with random train–test splits, which can overstate performance when closely related (homologous) sequences fall in both sets. We re-evaluated a widely used benchmark derived from the Protein Data Bank, with 40,211 unique protein sequences in ten functional classes. Six models were compared under random splits and under identity-controlled splits, which keep sequences sharing more than a set identity (90% down to 20%) on the same side: three k-mer composition classifiers, a method that copies the label of the most similar training sequence found by alignment, and two classifiers built on embeddings from the protein language model ESM-2. Under random splitting, 86.5% of test sequences had a training sequence more than 30% identical to them, and a nearest-neighbour model that only copies labels scored in the same range as the learned models. With related sequences kept apart at 30% identity, the k-mer classifiers lost about two-thirds of their macro-F 1 . As a secondary observation, alignment-based label transfer beat an ESM-2 classifier when close training sequences were available, and ESM-2 did better when they were removed; at 30% identity its macro-F 1 advantage was small and not statistically significant. The reason is unclear: almost every benchmark sequence has a close match in UniRef50, the database used to pretrain ESM-2, leaving too few test sequences distant from both the training set and the pretraining data to test generalization beyond them. Random-split results on this benchmark should not be taken as evidence of functional generalization, and comparisons involving protein language models must also account for pretraining data.
evidence_items.title: Homology Leakage Inflates Performance on a Protein Functional-Class Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine-learning forecasts of financial returns are usually judged by whether they beat other models, but in low signal-to-noise settings such comparisons can mislead. We propose an evaluation protocol for neural return forecasts that combines four elements: a zero-return benchmark with loss-based block-bootstrap tests and confidence bounds on the panel mean out-of-sample R²; an exact decomposition of R² into squared forecast–return alignment and an amplitude penalty; calibration that uses only past data; and the certainty-equivalent return of a mean–variance investor after transaction costs. We apply it to N-BEATS, N-HiTS and N-BEATSx on daily returns of 19 commodity futures from 2015 to 2026. No neural model improves significantly on zero, and the upper 95% bound on the mean daily R² is 0.16%. Training one network on all commodities raises the mean R² by 3.32 percentage points relative to separate training, yet almost all of this gain comes from smaller forecasts rather than a detectable improvement in alignment, and past-only calibration reduces it to 0.06 points. Sector-based pooling does no better than random grouping. Several forecasts raise the investor’s certainty-equivalent return over a historical-mean benchmark before costs, but none beats equal-weight buy-and-hold, the gains vanish at one-way costs above about 4 basis points, and the training strategy with the lowest loss is not the one with the highest certainty-equivalent return. Lower forecast loss relative to another model should therefore not be read as evidence of predictability or of economic value.
evidence_items.title: Neural Forecasting of Daily Commodity Futures Returns Against a Zero-Return Benchmark
