evidence_items.summary: Microlevel loss reserving can use claim-level information that aggregate methods such as chain ladder cannot exploit. This paper predicts individual ultimate claim amounts with a hybrid neural network that combines a feedforward network for static claim characteristics with a long short-term memory network for the payment history of each claim. The framework is evaluated on a simulated motor-insurance portfolio of claims closed at the final valuation date, so that predictions can be compared with known ultimates; the estimation of RBNS and IBNR reserves is outside the scope of the study. Severity strata are formed by k-means clustering of the ultimate amount, and covariates are selected with the Boruta algorithm, both fitted to the training claims only. With complete payment histories, the hybrid models produce much smaller aggregate deviations than chain ladder for recent accident years, while chain ladder remains competitive for mature ones. Boruta retains one or two covariates; the reduced set helps only the untuned full-portfolio model, whereas in the tuned severity-stratum models the full covariate set lowers the test MAE by one third to one half. In a backtest with payment histories truncated at December 2019, the hybrid models keep an accident-year MAPE of 2.1–3.0%, against 16.5% for chain ladder, but improve on the amount paid to date by only 10–15% for claims still open at that date. The results indicate that feature selection, segmentation, and model tuning should be evaluated jointly.
evidence_items.title: Predicting Individual Ultimate Claim Amounts with Hybrid Neural Networks and Claim Segmentation: A Benchmark for Microlevel Loss Reserving

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background: Insomnia is associated with a state of physiological hyperarousal rather thanwith a simple loss of sleep drive. Aromatherapy is used as self-care for this kind of sleepproblem, but its pharmacological basis is unclear. Linalyl acetate (LA) is a majorconstituent of bergamot and lavender oils. A recent study deposited brain transcriptomesfrom mice that inhaled LA and were sampled immediately after an acute stressor, andinterpreted a module of immediate-early genes (IEGs) as evidence of neurotrophin-drivenactivation, without reporting the direction of change. Methods: We reanalysed the deposited hippocampal and olfactory bulb microarrays(GSE316912, GSE316919; vehicle, 1% and 10% LA, n = 3 per group; tissue taken immediatelyafter the final tail suspension test) with a pre-specified 24-gene IEG set. Significance wasassessed with moderated t-statistics, competitive rank tests and exhaustive sample-labelpermutation (84 labellings). The LA profile was compared with public datasets for acutestress (GSE100236), sleep deprivation (GSE33302), chronic mild stress (GSE151807),chronic diazepam (GSE76700), chronic fluoxetine (GSE118669, GSE43261) and linaloolinhalation in rats (GSE19589, GSE90923). Results: Acute handling, restraint and cold swim each increased all 24 IEGs in thehippocampus, and sleep deprivation increased them. After LA inhalation the same geneswere decreased: 21 of 22 detected IEGs in the hippocampus and 22 of 23 in the olfactorybulb (label-permutation P = 0.012 and 0.024). LA therefore moved the stress-evokedactivation programme in the direction opposite to the acute stressors that induce it. Fourweeks of chronic mild stress, by contrast, also lowered these genes in all four brainregions examined, so the direction of the IEG programme depends on the duration of thestressor and does not by itself distinguish relief from chronic stress.
evidence_items.title: Olfactory receptor enrichment in fold-change rankings can arise without regulation: a null benchmark across 99 human transcriptomes

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Healthcare AI systems described as agentic may improve selected tasks, but gains can reflect models, information access, human support or complete intervention packages. We mapped clinical utility, safety and workflow consequences while distinguishing functional agency from evidence isolating its contribution. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by citation searches, through 11 September 2026. Eligible evidence comprised original empirical journal reports of healthcare systems described as agentic or demonstrating potentially agentic functions. Two authors independently screened records, and two independently extracted data, with adjudication. All four authors jointly assigned analytical classifications after a five-report pilot. A structured critical audit and descriptive Clinical Agency Evidence Chain informed synthesis. The review was not registered. Results: The corpus included 123 reports; 90 were classified as core or bounded functionally agentic. Within this subset, technical task performance was the endpoint category in 44/90 reports (48.9%), and clinical decision/process outcomes in 33/90 (36.7%). Three randomised reports in the broader corpus assessed patient health outcomes: one core, one boundary/non-agentic and one indeterminate. All evaluated bundled interventions. Evidence isolating agency and following its consequences within the same comparison was limited. Safety ascertainment, intended-user error correction and whole-pathway workload were incompletely reported. External or temporal validation occurred in 6/90 reports (6.7%), with partial validation in seven others. Predominantly retrospective, simulated or offline evidence limited clinical inference. Conclusions: Intervention-level benefit must be distinguished from the incremental contribution of agency. Technical gains and local or estimated time savings do not establish patient benefit or reduced total human work.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: A Scoping Review of Clinical Value, Safety, and Human Oversight

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise agentic AI systems exchange contextual information across functional modules, creating governance challenges when information crosses operational and organizational boundaries. This study distinguishes organizational governance boundaries from information exchange boundaries and proposes an Inter-Module Information Contract (IMIC) architecture for purpose-bounded context exchange. IMIC evaluates provenance, semantic and temporal validity, permitted information scope, and applicable originating constraints before downstream execution, independently of language-model reasoning. We compare IMIC with full-context sharing, reduced-context sharing, and strengthened structured handoff. In a deterministic benchmark of 32 synthetic conditions, joint correctness is achieved in 3, 10, 28, and 32 cases, respectively. The four differences between strengthened structured handoff and IMIC arise from conditions testing onward-transfer permission, recipient, purpose, and field scope. A downstream integration experiment evaluates 14 selected conditions across four local language models and three seeds, yielding 168 case–model–seed blocks and 672 method-level records. IMIC achieves correct exchange actions and information boundaries in all 168 blocks and joint correctness in 165 across four local LLMs and three seeds. Three permitted executions produce incorrect downstream responses despite correctly governed exchanges, demonstrating that information-exchange correctness does not guarantee correct downstream task performance. These results support the functional feasibility of the implemented originating-contract inheritance mechanism under controlled synthetic conditions. Further study is required to evaluate generalizability to independent enterprise workflows and richer policy structures and to extend the architecture to multiple originating providers, policy conflicts, and derived information.
evidence_items.title: Purpose-Bounded Context Exchange in Enterprise Agentic AI Systems: An Inter-Module Information Contract Architecture

evidence_items.summary: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.
evidence_items.title: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.
evidence_items.title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Learned image compression (LIC) papers often report BD-rate improvements of only a few percent. They are measured against VTM reference software whose version keeps changing: the claims we audit name 7 versions, 5 in 2025 papers alone. But how comparable are these numbers across papers, and what evidence should future papers give for such small gains? We introduce LIC-Audit, an analysis of 353 released rate-distortion curves from 36 repositories, and a controlled re-evaluation of eight public codec releases with 28,193 encode-decode records. We identify three problems. First, different VTM reference runs change BD-rates by up to 3.56 percentage points, and on CLIC Pro published numbers order 10 of 55 method pairs differently from a common computation; comparing codecs directly over a fixed quality range removes this dependence. Second, releases use different and mostly undocumented conventions for counting bits, computing PSNR, and padding images. Under consistent measurement, the GLIC method's 1.00% lead over the HPCM method on Tecnick becomes a 1.43% deficit, changing only the padding reverses the comparison of HPCM and CMIC, and most gaps narrow when MS-SSIM replaces PSNR. Third, average curves hide how much results vary from image to image, so whether a small gain is statistically significant depends on the assumed variation. An optimistic assumption calls 12.0% of comparisons between equally good codecs significant on test sets as small as Kodak, instead of 5%; a cautious one leaves 18 of 45 differences between recent codecs undecided, yet per-image results show 12 of them to be significant. Beyond auditing past results, LIC-Audit provides a versioned evaluation protocol, a public leaderboard website with a scoring tool, source-linked benchmark data, per-image measurements, and reporting guidelines, to help future LIC papers make comparable and verifiable claims of progress.
evidence_items.title: LIC-Audit: How Comparable Are Reported Gains in Learned Image Compression?

evidence_items.summary: A coding agent is a language model inside a harness: the system prompt, the tools, and the context management that let a chat model work in a repository. Most of the engineering on these agents goes into the harness, and vendors and leaderboards credit it with score gains. Earlier studies have fixed the model and swapped the harness, but have not measured whether the swap changes the pass rate more than running the same harness again. We run seven models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified and two benchmarks of other kinds, and rerun them unchanged. No harness leads consistently across models. Where the data can bound the difference between two harnesses, the bound is 2 to 5 points, and a harness swap changes about as many task outcomes as a rerun. The exceptions are harness effects in particular pairings of model and harness, whose direction changes with the model: OpenCode trails by 8 to 9 points on one model and leads by 14 on another. Cost differences between harnesses also depend on the model, from under 10% to 3 to 4 times. Which harness is better therefore has no answer apart from the model, and a harness difference should be reported next to a rerun.
evidence_items.title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly

evidence_items.summary: Biomedical tables often combine thousands of measured variables with only tens or hundreds of labelled samples, a regime that is poorly represented in general-purpose tabular benchmarks. We introduce TabBench-Bio, a living and interactive benchmark of 43 biomedical datasets spanning multiple domains. Under a shared cross-validation protocol, we compare classical estimators, neural networks, and tabular foundation models across 28 feature-by-sample operating points. At the reference cell of 10,000 features and 100 training samples, RealTabPFN 2.5 has the highest point estimate, closely followed by TabPFN 3 and Logistic Regression. A paired bootstrap over the target pool separates RealTabPFN 2.5 from TabPFN 3 by 87 Elo (95\% interval [43, 129]). Tabular foundation models generally occupy the leading ranks, while the strongest configuration depends on the operating point and biomedical modality. The AutoML framework AutoGluon, using its one-hour "extreme" preset, is configured as a separate resource-intensive reference and reported here at the reference and full cell. Fold-level predictions, run status, and deterministic aggregations make every reported result reproducible and reusable. The benchmark is open to contributions of new biomedical datasets. The interactive leaderboard is available at https://tabbench-bio.eu.
evidence_items.title: TabBench-Bio: A Living Benchmark for Machine Learning on High-Dimensional Biomedical Tables

evidence_items.summary: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.
evidence_items.title: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development

Voipan and M. Barbu, submitted to the Journal of Process Control). Version 3 contains only the experiments reported in the article and its supplementary material, including those added in revision. The plant is the open-source bsm2-python implementation (v0.0.16) of Benchmark Simulation Model No. 2 with its official 609-day influent; no other data are needed. Every simulation uses a corrected dissolved-oxygen PI loop (integral accumulated), enabled with BSM2 DO PI=accum; README.md explains why. Contents - analysis/: recomputes the paper from the included run data. verify.py recomputes every reported value and fails on any drift; make supp tables.py and figures/make figures.py regenerate the supplementary tables and Figures 1-4; figures/matlab/ redraws the same figures in MATLAB. Requires only NumPy and Matplotlib. - code/: the closed-loop driver, surrogate and policy training, screening experiments and scenario generation, with the launch scripts that record the exact flags of every reported run; code/review/ holds the experiments added in revision (stress influents, held-out decision test, recirculation step, severity, level-guarded release rule, sign-only ablation arm). - checkpoints/: the trained surrogates and policies the paper reports, including the sixteen arms of the ablation grid. - runs/: the raw full-year runs reduced by the analysis, and the logs of every run the paper uses. evidence_items.summary: Background We developed a hospital web application that searches 266 destinations and links results to indoor navigation. Its default retrieval tiers run locally; an optional cloud large language model (LLM) tier requires explicit invocation. Synthetic queries were used because default-tier searches are not server-logged. Objective We examined how post hoc review of an LLM-generated benchmark changed the apparent benefit of completed system updates. Methods Version v2 added pronunciation aliases to v1; v3 added colloquial knowledge, pronunciation forms, destination-level score combination, and false-match rules. Two v3 rules were informed by evaluation-query failures. A clinician and a medical administrative coauthor jointly reviewed 563 synthetic queries without blinding, excluding 129 and rewriting 289 under review-defined policies. The final data contained 401 answerable and 33 no-valid-destination queries. Archived versions were compared across sequential review stages and with lexical and embedding implementations. Results Among the same 192 answerable evaluation-query identifiers and final accepted destinations, rewriting increased top-1 accuracy from 43.8% to 62.0% for v1 and from 56.8% to 63.0% for v3. Their difference remained near 13 percentage points through earlier review stages and decreased to 1.0 point at rewriting. The tested multilingual-E5-small implementation achieved higher top-3 accuracy than v3 (87.0% vs. 69.3%; exploratory P &lt; 0.001), with differences in passage scoring, abstention, and evidence display. For v3, candidate returns occurred on 4/11 reviewed no-valid-destination evaluation queries and 11/29 original queries in a retrospective sensitivity analysis. Conclusions Unblinded benchmark editing changed performance estimates for frozen systems within this synthetic corpus. The findings do not establish improved real-user performance, independent generalization, or comparative clinical safety.
evidence_items.title: Changes in apparent system performance after post hoc human review of a large language model-generated benchmark for hospital wayfinding search: a comparative methodological evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Volumetric image registration is a fundamental computer vision problem with broad applications across fields such as medicine, biological and cellular imaging, geoscience, and cultural heritage preservation. The 3D image registration problem is commonly divided into monomodal and multimodal registration problems, depending on whether the images originate from the same or different imaging modalities. Monomodal 3D image registration is a well-studied problem with established state-of-the-art methods and a range of widely recognized benchmarks. In contrast, multimodal 3D image registration remains an open problem despite numerous developed registration methods. A key challenge is that existing open-access multimodal benchmark datasets are scarce and limited in modality diversity, which constrains registration generalization across modalities. As a result, most multimodal registration methods remain tuned to specific modalities and narrow domains of objects. This leads to the need to redevelop multimodal registration tools for each specific task, and no universal solution exists. To approach the task of universal multimodal image registration, in this paper we introduce STAMM3D (Similarity Transform Alignment of Multimodal 3D images)—a new benchmark for multimodal registration that includes an open-access dataset of 22 3D images of rigid medical, biological, and non-biomedical objects and provides an automated Target Registration Error-based evaluation framework. The publicly availablebenchmark offers a high-resolution dataset with multiple domains of objects and a wide range of different modalities deliberately chosen to test and compare universality and generalization properties of the registration methods. The focus of the dataset is on non-deformable image registration since it directly affects the quality of image fusion, whether used independently or within multi-stage deformable registration pipelines.
evidence_items.title: STAMM3D: Dataset and Benchmark for Non-Deformable 3D Image Registration in Multiple Modalities

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Computational methods for virtual screening and lead optimization are benchmarked on specifically designed data sets to predict compound potency. Here we present a workflow and two resulting new benchmark data sets, BALLROOM A and BALLROOM S, from combining PDB and ChEMBL data. Due to high data quality standards, the formation of molecule pairs measured under the same conditions only, and avoiding pairs with close to equal potency, we achieve a reliable data collection for physics-based bioactivity prediction based on protein–ligand complex structures. When testing state-of-the-art scoring functions for docking, no classical method statistically outperforms a simple molecular-weight-based prediction, consistent with previous studies such as D3R. While challenging for physics-based methods, the prediction task can be easily addressed by simple nearest-neigbor scorers showing that the benchmark cannot be used for machine learing based scoring functions due to significant train-test inference.

evidence_items.summary: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by generating a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these rendered proxy videos and the complex, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene generation: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether facts that pass the rules are recognizable in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.
evidence_items.title: VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.
evidence_items.title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?

evidence_items.summary: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations \rev{through separate per-player decision calls}, selecting high-level actions \rev{and image-labeled target cells} while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of \rev{two-player} coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding\rev{; text gives no station coordinates, so target locations come mainly from the image}. The evaluation compares \rev{five VLMs and a privileged scripted reference policy on all 20 maps}, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, \rev{aim accuracy}, and model API expenditure. \rev{Two paired ablations on all 20 maps toggle a shared self-authored notebook and reduce the textual prompt from about 3,600 to about 440 words while keeping the images fixed.} \rev{The strongest model completes 35\% of orders and exceeds the scripted reference, which has ground-truth station access; the notebook's effect is mixed in sign and not statistically reliable, and reducing the prompt text lowers the score of two models while leaving the other three nearly unchanged.} Together, the environment design and evaluation protocol provide a framework for investigating how visual state tracking and task scheduling contribute to coordinated cooking behavior.
evidence_items.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination

evidence_items.summary: As AI systems are increasingly used to draft radiology reports, reliably evaluating their clinical quality remains a critical challenge. We introduce RadMatch, a multi-stage LLM-based framework that turns report evaluation into a structured, auditable finding-level record. It extracts findings from a reference and a candidate report, matches them by clinical equivalence, grades each match over ten clinical attributes, and gives every match and unmatched finding a verdict and a clinical-significance tier. To validate metrics on CT, we build and release MetricEval-BodyCT, the first public metric-evaluation benchmark of chest and abdomen CT reports annotated by radiologists error by error. On it and three chest X-ray benchmarks, RadMatch with an open 31B judge on consumer GPUs agrees with radiologists more closely than previous published metrics, and even reaches inter-expert agreement on ReXVal and on the significant errors of MetricEval-BodyCT. Radiologists auditing its decisions on 60 studies confirm 98.5% of its matches and 93.6% of the errors it counts. When used to evaluate state-of-the-art radiology report generation models, RadMatch shows that most CT models, unlike several chest X-ray models, actually leave more significant errors than an image-blind normal template, as their added unsupported findings outnumber the reference findings they correctly report. We provide RadMatch's code, its dashboard, the MetricEval-BodyCT dataset and all per-report scores.
evidence_items.title: RadMatch: Auditable Radiology Report Evaluation via Finding-Level Matching

evidence_items.summary: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.
evidence_items.title: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?

evidence_items.summary: Political bias in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly significant, but difficult to measure reproducibly across political and linguistic contexts. We introduce Polar, a 4,026-instance multiple-choice benchmark that measures political bias through option-level likelihoods rather than prompt-based generation. Polar covers two ideological axes and eight issue categories derived from the Manifesto Project, and evaluates models in parallel across U.S. and South Korean political contexts. Across 38 LLMs, measured bias varies systematically with political context, issue category, model group, and presentation language. All models lean left-progressive on U.S. political content, but show more centered and mixed patterns on South Korean content. Translation experiments further show that presentation language alone can shift measured bias. These findings highlight the need for multilingual and cross-contextual evaluation of political bias in LLMs. The code and dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/mcrl/Polar) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/thunder-research-group/Polar).
evidence_items.title: Polar: A Benchmark for Evaluating Political Bias in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Surgical resection remains the only potentially curative treatment for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), and eligibility depends on accurate assessment of vascular invasion (VI), i.e., tumor extension into adjacent critical vessels. Despite its importance for preoperative staging and surgical planning, computational VI assessment remains underexplored. Two major challenges are the lack of public datasets and the diagnostic ambiguity at the tumor-vessel interface, which leads to substantial inter-rater variability even among expert radiologists. To address these limitations, we introduce the CURVAS-PDACVI Dataset and Challenge, an open benchmark for uncertainty-aware AI in PDAC staging based on a densely annotated dataset with five independent expert annotations per scan. We also propose a multi-metric evaluation framework that extends beyond spatial overlap to include probabilistic calibration and VI assessment. Evaluation of six state-of-the-art methods shows that strong global volumetric overlap does not necessarily translate into reliable performance at clinically critical tumor-vessel interfaces. In particular, methods optimized for binary segmentation perform competitively on average overlap metrics, but often degrade in high-complexity cases with low expert consensus, either collapsing in volume or overextending at uncertain boundaries. In contrast, methods that model inter-rater disagreement produce better calibrated probabilistic maps and show greater robustness in these ambiguous cases. The benchmark highlights the limitations of volumetric accuracy as a proxy for localized surgical utility, motivating uncertainty-aware probabilistic models for preoperative decision-making.
evidence_items.title: CURVAS-PDACVI: A Multi-Rater CT Dataset and Challenge for Pancreatic Cancer Segmentation and Vascular Involvement Assessme

evidence_items.summary: Humans can look at a static scene and instantly predict what happens next -- will moving this object cause a collision? We call this ability Causal Spatial Reasoning. However, current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot do this, as they remain largely restricted to static spatial perception, struggling to answer "what-if" questions in a 3D scene. We introduce CausalSpatial, a diagnostic benchmark evaluating whether models can anticipate consequences of object motions across four tasks: Collision, Compatibility, Occlusion, and Trajectory. Results expose a severe gap: humans score 84% while GPT-5 achieves only 54%. Why do MLLMs fail? Our analysis uncovers a fundamental deficiency: models over-rely on textual chain-of-thought reasoning that drifts from visual evidence, producing fluent but spatially ungrounded hallucinations. To address this, we propose the Causal Object World model (COW), a framework that externalizes the simulation process by generating videos of hypothetical dynamics. With explicit visual cues of causality, COW enables models to ground their reasoning in physical reality rather than linguistic priors. We make the dataset and code publicly available here: https://github.com/CausalSpatial/CausalSpatial
evidence_items.title: CausalSpatial: A Benchmark for Object-Centric Causal Spatial Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been used to generate mutants both in the research community and in industrial practice. However, there has been no comprehensive empirical study of their performance for this increasingly important LLM-based Software Engineering application. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study evaluating both a wide range of traditional approaches and LLM-based approaches. Particularly, we evaluate BugFarm, LLMorpheus, and our newly designed prompt for mutant generation. The experiments cover both leading open and closed source LLMs, on 851 real bugs from 2 Java real-world bug benchmarks. Our results reveal that, compared to existing traditional approaches, LLMs generate more diverse mutants that are behaviorally closer to real bugs and, most importantly, achieve a 1.8 \(\times\) improvement in real bug detection, defined as the proportion of real bugs whose faulty behaviors can be mimicked by at least one generated mutant. Specifically, LLM-based approaches reach a detection rate of 77.4%, compared to 41.6% for rule-based techniques, representing an absolute gain of 35.8 percentage points. Nevertheless, our results also reveal that these impressive improvements in effectiveness come at a cost: LLM-generated mutants exhibit worse non-compilability, duplication, and equivalent mutant rates than rule-based approaches by 25.9, 7.1, and 2.6 percentage points, respectively. These findings provide actionable insights for both research and practice. They allow practitioners to have greater confidence in deploying LLM-based mutation, while researchers now have a baseline for the state-of-the-art, with which they can research techniques to further improve effectiveness and reduce cost.
evidence_items.title: A Comprehensive Study on Large Language Models for Mutation Testing

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.
evidence_items.title: HandWorldBench: A Unified Benchmark for Hand-Centric World Models

evidence_items.summary: Widely used category discovery benchmarks have become increasingly saturated and often fail to reflect real-world discovery settings, making long-term evaluation of new methods difficult. We introduce PS-SPLIT, a large-scale fine-grained benchmark for category discovery, motivated by taxonomic splitting: the real-world process by which what was once considered a single species is found to comprise multiple distinct ones. PS-SPLIT contains 79K globally distributed, high-quality, community-collected bird images spanning 771 species, derived from 257 recent real expert-verified taxonomic splits, with associated geographic metadata and full taxonomic hierarchy. The visual differences between categories arising from real taxonomic splits can be very subtle, often requiring significant human expertise to tell apart, making PS-SPLIT a challenging benchmark which we hope will assist in advancing fine-grained category discovery research. Based on taxonomic splitting, we introduce the task of discovery by category splitting, where the goal is to determine which known categories should be subdivided into new finer-grained subcategories. We adapt four generalized category discovery methods to this setting, evaluate existing methods, and show that there is substantial room for future progress.
evidence_items.title: Predicting Species Splits: A Challenging Fine-Grained Benchmark for Category Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Domain adaptation for semantic segmentation is challenging when target-domain images are unavailable during training. Zero-shot domain adaptation addresses this by adapting models using only textual descriptions of the target domain. However, existing prompt-learning methods are not well suited for ResNet-based CLIP vision backbones or pixel-level cross-modal feature alignment. We propose CROMPT, a prompt-learning framework for zero-shot domain adaptation in semantic segmentation. CROMPT introduces Cross-Modal Feature Augmentation (CROMA), combining Random Visual Prompting with Hybrid Textual Prompting (HTP) to jointly adapt visual and textual representations. We further propose CROMA-VL, which leverages vision-language models to generate domain-conditioned prompts, and a progressive easy-to-hard adaptation strategy for improved domain invariance. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods, achieving 1.63-2.63% mIoU gains while maintaining inference-time complexity. These results establish CROMPT as an effective and efficient framework for zero-shot multi-domain semantic segmentation. OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=FxqFsIL685
evidence_items.title: CROMPT: Adapting CLIP via Cross-Modal Prompting for Robust Zero-Shot Generalization under Adverse Weather

evidence_items.summary: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark need not require another large model. We use public evaluation counts to choose a weak Beta prior, then update it exactly from at most 31 revealed outcomes. The predictor uses no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. Its single online evaluation in the AIMS competition returned a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference. The complete submission is 7,754 bytes; a server microbenchmark measures 12.71 microseconds per prediction with 31 matching labels. We describe how source evaluations are compressed into 301 prior means and show why a concentration of two lets new evidence rapidly determine the prediction. The resulting posterior gives exact uncertainty about the modelled success rate without numerical integration or neural inference. A public evaluation covers 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds, reaching Brier ALC 0.200250 for the submitted method. Accompanying code and sufficient statistics reconstruct the fitted prior byte for byte and replay all 632 evaluation trajectories. The result demonstrates how much predictive value a compact Bayesian model can extract from sparse target feedback at very low online cost.
evidence_items.title: Fast Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty Quantification in Sparse AI Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Video-to-4D mesh generation has made substantial progress in recovering dynamic 3D geometry and motion from monocular videos. However, commonly used feed-forward approaches remain prone to sticking artifacts, where geodesically distant vertices move together incorrectly when they become spatially close. We attribute this failure to cross-part motion leakage: spatially nearby yet structurally distant vertices may retrieve similar motion information when motion decoding fails to distinguish spatial proximity from mesh connectivity. To address this issue, we introduce TRoPE, a topology-aware relative positional encoding that makes mesh connectivity explicit in the interaction between vertex queries and mesh-supported motion sources. TRoPE derives spectral features from the graph Laplacian and constructs pairwise topological relations from distances between multi-scale diffusion features, using these relations to modulate vertex--anchor attention through rotary phases. We further introduce a vertex-wise tail-risk objective that emphasizes persistently high-error vertices to explicitly suppress sticking artifacts. To better characterize and quantify these failures, we introduce MeshSticking-4D, a dedicated benchmark for this failure mode. Experiments on MeshSticking-4D show that TRoPE suppresses sticking artifacts while improving overall motion accuracy. Compared with the baseline, it reduces the worst-vertex error by 39.4% and lowers the separation failure rate from 49.35% to 34.90%. Additional evaluations on Motion-80 and Motion324-Subset show lower tail errors on diverse objects, while transfer to Mesh4D demonstrates applicability across backbones.
evidence_items.title: TRoPE: Topology-aware Relative Positional Encoding for 4D Generation

evidence_items.summary: Inferring the unseen side of a 3D assembly requires reasoning about part placement and occlusion. Different assemblies can match the observed views while producing different hidden views, leaving the target ambiguous. We introduce SixthView, a benchmark in which models predict a sixth orthographic view from five observed views and information about the component shapes. The benchmark contains 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2--10 parts and requires a dense grid of part labels for the missing view, allowing both exact-view and cell-level evaluation. For each item, we exhaustively verify that all legal assemblies consistent with the exact component geometry and observed label grids yield the same target view. With these inputs, the task tests symbolic assembly and coordinate reasoning. The image-only variants additionally require shape recovery from rendered views, where occlusion can make different 3D shapes look identical. We evaluate three vision-language models under four input conditions. Across 552 items with complete evaluations, exact-grid accuracy with images plus exact text ranges from 33.2% to 85.4%. Adding exact text to separate images improves accuracy by 19.7--63.0 percentage points, whereas adding images to exact text changes it by only $-0.5$ to $+2.1$ points. Separate image panels outperform a merged sheet by 6.7--11.1 points. The results show that performance depends strongly on access to exact symbolic information, with little further improvement from images once the geometry is specified. GitHub: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sixthview_benchmark
evidence_items.title: SixthView: A Benchmark for Hidden-View Reconstruction and 3D Assembly Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.
evidence_items.title: TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery

evidence_items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.
evidence_items.title: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Repository-level migration requires more than translating isolated functions: it must preserve behaviour across modules, shared state, build structure, and dependencies. Existing translation benchmarks predominantly cover small programs or small repositories, or fixed and widely studied language pairs. We present f2x50, a target-independent benchmark comprising 50 public Fortran repositories pinned to exact Git revisions. It contains 12,116 Git-tracked Fortran files and 6,569,806 lines, divided into three structural-complexity tiers and paired with 561 deterministic behavioural probes. Of these probes, 446 compile pinned source files with small drivers and span 131 repository--routine pairs. Every repository has at least five direct checks that collectively execute at least two routines. f2x50 provides target-independent tools for acquisition, validation, licence review, and reproducibility, together with a reference adapter for evaluating Python targets. The remaining probes are explicitly classified as extractions, inline reimplementations, or synthetic fixtures. The benchmark therefore supports comparable evaluations across migration tools and target languages.
evidence_items.title: f2x50: A Repository-Scale Benchmark for Fortran-to-X Software Migration

evidence_items.summary: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1times less data and >120times fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.
evidence_items.title: LogT: Logically Think with Images for Visual Search

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides a reproducible numerical benchmark for evaluating reduced-order approximations of unilateral contact between a pressurized hyperelastic spherical membrane and a rigid plane. The benchmark comprises six pressure–mesh configurations, combining three inflation pressures (4, 8, and 12 psi) with two meridional discretizations (64 and 128 elements). Nine evaluation loads are considered for each configuration, resulting in 54 test states and 270 comparative records for five numerical approximation methods: PCHIP interpolation, POD, contact-local POD, a spectral reduced basis, and a contact-enriched nonlinear reduced-order model (KM02C). The dataset contains numerical results from the full-order reference model, reduced-order calculations, nodal state arrays, reconstructed contact reactions, training states, diagnostic indicators, and supporting Python scripts. Particular attention is given to distinguishing global reaction-force closure from local equilibrium accuracy. The data enable researchers to examine residual equilibrium errors, contact localization, active contact sets, sensitivity to diagnostic thresholds, and the performance of reduced-order approximations. The archive includes documentation, data dictionaries, verification procedures, and source code supporting computational reproducibility. The dataset represents numerical solutions of a specified discrete shell–gas contact model. It does not constitute experimental validation or establish mesh-independent continuum contact-pressure predictions.
evidence_items.title: Numerical benchmark dataset for reduced-order unilateral contact of pressurized hyperelastic membranes

evidence_items.summary: Medium-chain dehydrogenases/reductases are highly versatile oxidoreductases with broad industrial relevance but complex structure-function relationships that continue to challenge catalytic performance prediction. A Benchmark for Medium-Chain Dehydrogenases (MCDBench) is introduced as a rigorously curated benchmark dataset comprising 792 enzyme-substrate-cofactor combinations, including experimentally validated inactive cases obtained under standardized conditions. MCDBench spans 36 chemically diverse alcohol substrates, representative MDR subclasses, and multiple cofactor types, enabling systematic evaluation of model generalization. Benchmarking four representative activity-prediction models (DLKcat, UniKP, TurNuP, and CataPro) shows that correlations with experimental activities remain modest under standardized conditions, and that distinguishing active from inactive catalytic space remains a practical challenge across enzyme classes and substrate types. Analysis points to a positive-data skew inherited from widely used biochemical databases and the relative scarcity of validated negative samples as key factors shaping this behavior. By providing a standardized benchmark that integrates experimentally validated negative cases, MCDBench offers a unified experimental and computational framework to help the field measure and further improve the discrimination of active and inactive catalytic space for biocatalyst design.
evidence_items.title: Precision in Predicting Catalytic Performance of Medium Chain Dehydrogenase: A Benchmark Data Set and Comparative Metrics

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.
evidence_items.title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games

evidence_items.summary: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/
evidence_items.title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: This preprint presents Lesion-Net, a two-dimensional hierarchical transformer for ischemic stroke lesion segmentation in diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI). The framework investigates whether preserving spatial detail and allocating greater encoder capacity to high-resolution stages can improve segmentation in patients with low lesion burden. Its architecture combines reduced early downsampling, greater early-stage depth, uniform channel widths, a multiscale decoder, and a feature-fusion segmentation head. Lesion-Net was evaluated on the ISLES 2022 and Johns Hopkins University Stroke (JHUS) datasets using DWI-only inputs and patient-level training, validation, and test partitions. It achieved overall Dice Similarity Coefficient scores of 79.82% on ISLES 2022 and 77.14% on JHUS. Patient-level burden analysis showed the highest small-burden Dice scores among the evaluated methods, reaching 81.80% and 80.32%, respectively. Architectural ablations examined the effects of spatial resolution, encoder-depth allocation, and channel configuration. The findings support adapting hierarchical encoder capacity to lesion characteristics. Lower performance relative to leading comparators in medium- and large-burden groups highlights a specialization trade-off and motivates further evaluation of lesion-level detection, cross-dataset generalization, and computational efficiency.
evidence_items.title: Lesion-Net: A Lesion-aware Hierarchical Transformer for Ischemic Stroke Segmentation in DWI

evidence_items.summary: The loan approval process is a vital process within the Banking industry. A variety of factors are taken into consideration when approving a loan to an applicant. These include income, age, experience in employment, credit score, loan amount requested, education, property ownership, and previous loan history. Machine learning can be used to analyse the data and predict whether an application will be approved or denied. This research contains two parts. Part A contains a dataset with 45,000 entries of loan applications. This dataset includes a variety of information about the applicant including income, employment, credit score, loan amount, reason for loan, etc. The target column indicates whether the loan has been approved or denied. Various machine learning classification models such as Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM) can be applied to the dataset. These can then be compared using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score to see which machine learning model works best for predicting loan approvals. Part B of the research looks at comparing the lending rates of different banks using data provided by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The term loan rates for different banks can be compared. This can be simplified by looking at a set loan amount and time period. We can then calculate the estimated monthly EMI using the lending rates. This will help us understand how varying lending rates can impact the monthly repayment amount. This research combines machine learning to predict loan approvals and comparing lending rates. evidence_items.summary: Public brain tumour MRI collections are routinely reported with near-perfect classification accuracy, yet they carry no patient identifiers and their train/test overlap is rarely quantified. We present a duplicate-aware, reproducible frozen-feature benchmark on BRISC 2025 (6000 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted slices; glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, no tumour). A perceptual-hash audit found 1352 candidate near-duplicate pairs, with 439 of them crossing the official train/test split, and 104 training images that are pixel-identical to test images; a visual review of sampled pairs showed that most candidates were other slices of the same scan, with an estimated 5–10% false matches. Removing redundant copies and every training image connected to the test set left 5477 images, a split that is duplicate-aware but not patient-independent. Under an identical linear probe, ImageNet-supervised ResNet-18/50 and self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14 were competitive: DINOv2 was numerically ahead (macro-F1 77.3 ± 0.1%, macro-AUROC 93.2%), but no pairwise difference survived Holm correction. In-pool validation overstated official test macro-F1 by 9.7–13.5 points; control experiments showed that this gap is not an artefact of the filtering but mainly reflects a distribution difference between the official partitions. Meningioma recall stayed at 50–53%, and all linear heads were under-confident. We release the splits, audit tables and per-image predictions.
evidence_items.title: Validation Is Not Enough: A Duplicate-Aware, Reproducible Frozen-Feature Benchmark for Brain Tumour MRI Classification on BRISC 2025

evidence_items.summary: Agents can expand the covariate space of randomized experiments by retrieving fast-moving local context missed by slow-changing survey baseline covariates, helping characterize who benefits most from an intervention. Verifying such covariates is difficult: individual treatment effects are unobserved, retrieval leakage can pull post-treatment information into nominally pretreatment summaries, and encoder leakage can inject post-treatment pretraining knowledge into representations even after temporal filtering of inputs. Guided by a two-channel information bound separating summary provenance from encoder weights, we propose a three-layer benchmark protocol: (i) retrieval admissibility via pre-treatment date filtering; (ii) heterogeneity validation scored rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs); and (iii) encoder admissibility checked with chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes, and weight perturbations. Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, we compare session-isolated retrieval (sandboxed, bounded-budget agent runs per study) against a persistent workspace teammate (xAI's GrokBot) that builds one date-verified corpus per study while blinded to outcomes. The workspace teammate yields higher mean RATE ratios in 6/11 datasets for text alone and 7 for combined features, though paired tests show neither workflow universally dominates. Even on fixed retrieved text, encoder choice significantly shifts heterogeneity signal. Chronologically vintaged probes show no clear evidence of weight leakage, but single-record adapter perturbation analyses show that memorized future facts, once present, persist until injected noise degrades model output. Temporal filtering of retrieval is necessary but insufficient: verifying agent-generated covariates requires jointly examining source provenance, out-of-sample treatment-effect signal, and encoder weights.
evidence_items.title: Agent Verifiers in Counterfactual Analysis: A Pilot Study Benchmarking Agentic Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) aim to generate and understand human-like text by leveraging deep learning and natural language processing techniques. In software development, LLMs can enhance the coding experience through coding automation, reducing development time and improving code quality. Code refactoring is a technique used to enhance the internal quality of the code base without altering its external functionalities. Leveraging LLMs for code refactoring can help developers improve code quality with minimal effort. This article presents an empirical study evaluating the quality of refactored code produced by StarCoder2, GPT-4o Mini, GPT-4o, LLaMA 3, and DeepSeek-v3. Specifically, we (1) evaluate whether the code refactored by the LLMs can improve code quality, (2) understand the differences between the types of refactoring applied by the different LLMs and compare their effectiveness, and (3) evaluate whether the quality of the refactored code generated by the LLM can be improved through one-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting. We analyze the refactoring capabilities of LLMs on 30 open source Java projects. We evaluate StarCoder2, LLaMA 3, GPT-4o Mini, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-v3 on their ability to improve static code quality metrics, pass unit tests, and reduce code smells. Our findings reveal that production-grade models such as GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 achieve pass@5 unit test success rates above 90% on multi-file refactorings. LLaMA 3 achieves the highest overall code smell reduction with a median reduction of 15.1%, while DeepSeek-v3 and GPT-4o achieve the greatest improvements in cohesion, coupling, and complexity. StarCoder2 demonstrates strengths in modularity improvements and systematic refactorings. Developers outperform LLMs in complex, context-sensitive refactorings such as attribute encapsulation.
evidence_items.title: An Empirical Study on the Code Refactoring Capability of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning prediction of antibody-antigen binding affinity depends as much on the training data as on the model, yet public affinity measurements are scattered across databases with incompatible formats, mix genuine dissociation constants with censored or predicted values, and concentrate most of their label mass on a few heavily mutated targets. We present GRABS (Geometric Resource for Antibody Binding Studies), a curated, content-addressed, structure-ready dataset that consolidates nine public sources, of which the seven with redistributable licenses yield 4,380 canonical antibody-antigen records} (median-collapsed from 4,761 raw measurements), each with an experimentally measured dissociation constant (K d ), paired heavy and light variable regions (VH, VL), and an antigen sequence, covering 2,015 distinct antigen sequences. Every structure, graph, and feature is addressed by a content key, md5(VH+VL+antigen)[:10], and verified non-circularly: each graph's node features are decoded back to sequence and re-hashed, matching the content key for 4,282/4,282 (100%) structure-backed records. This integrity is load-bearing: an alignment ablation shows that a previously-reported strong cross-target result (R 2 ≈ 0.415) was a misalignment-mediated source/batch leak that content-key regeneration dissolves. On the resulting leak-free, antigen-cluster-grouped benchmark, cross-target ranking of variants of a held-out antigen collapses to the noise floor (within-held-out-antigen Spearman ρ ≈ 0 for every model family: sequence, structure, and folding-confidence), with structure giving no advantage, a rigorously leakage-controlled quantification of the limited reach of current methods.
evidence_items.title: GRABS: a content-addressed antibody-antigen binding-affinity dataset with predicted structures and a leak-free benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-M) is a rare but often fatal immune-related adverse event. Large language models (LLMs) have provided new opportunities for patient education, yet whether they can effectively support patient education in ICI-M remains unknown. In this study, we submitted 20 standardized ICI-M-related patient questions to five LLMs (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5 Flash, DeepSeek-V4, Qwen 3.7, and Doubao), generating 100 responses. Model performance was evaluated using the Global Quality Score (GQS), modified DISCERN (mDISCERN), Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI), Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP), Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool understandability and actionability scores (PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A), and six readability indices. Significant inter-model differences were observed across most quality and readability metrics, and no single model outperformed the others across all dimensions. DeepSeek-V4 achieved the highest mDISCERN score [5.00 (IQR, 4.00–5.00)], whereas ChatGPT-5.5 achieved the highest PEMAT-A score [40.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00)]. Readability was suboptimal, with a mean FKGL of 16.60 ± 2.64. Correlation analyses demonstrated information quality, usability, and readability represented correlated but distinct evaluation dimensions. While LLMs may serve as adjunctive tools for ICI-M patient education, substantial optimization of content accessibility and actionability is required prior to clinical implementation.
evidence_items.title: Quality, reliability, and readability of large language model responses to questions about immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis: A cross-sectional study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reliable preoperative classification and outcome prediction could improve management of locally advanced colorectal cancer. We retrospectively studied 879 participants from two centers, including 741 patients with locally advanced colorectal cancer and 138 with benign colorectal lesions. Clinical, radiomics, deep learning, and early fusion models were trained at center A ( n = 615) and independently tested at center B ( n = 264) using pretreatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography and clinical data. The clinical-radiomics nomogram achieved a test AUC of 0.957 for benign-malignant classification. For 3-year and 5-year overall survival, radiomics achieved test AUCs of 0.874 and 0.898, while fusion achieved 0.870 and 0.899, respectively. These findings identify CT radiomics as a promising digital biomarker for colorectal cancer stratification and show that early deep learning fusion offers limited incremental value over an optimized radiomics baseline.
evidence_items.title: Multicenter evaluation of radiomics and multimodal artificial intelligence for colorectal cancer diagnosis and survival prediction

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping doctoral education, yet few empirically evaluated pedagogical models integrate AI literacy with research and teaching competence. This study examined changes associated with implementing the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model, which positions doctoral candidates who are also university teachers as co-researchers of their own research and teaching practice under an explicit responsible-AI framework. A participatory action research design with convergent triangulation was implemented during the 2025–2026 academic year. Thirty-four doctoral candidates participated in four collaborative virtual workshops organised through cycles of planning, action, observation and critical reflection. Self-report measures administered at three time points were integrated with interviews, focus groups, observation notes, reflective logbooks and independently verified academic products. Self-reported research competence, AI-supported digital competence and creative-pedagogical competence increased significantly between each pair of measurement points (pre–post dₐᵥ = 1.83, 2.10 and 1.69, respectively). All participants integrated generative AI into at least one university course, and 76.5% implemented a sustained course redesign. Because the design lacked a comparison group and relied on perceived competence, maturation, testing effects, response-shift bias and the programme’s ordinary activities may also account for the changes. The findings are therefore associative rather than causal and constitute preliminary evidence that warrants controlled replication in other doctoral contexts.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Doctoral Education: A Participatory Action Research Evaluation of the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model
