evidence_items.summary: Abstract The interpretation of neutron scattering data remains a major bottleneck in materials discovery, as it demands an iterative cycle of data reduction, modeling, and refinement. That is too time-consuming for experts and too complex for novices. Here we introduce DrSai-Rongzai, an autonomous agent built on a large language model (LLM) that perfoms joint neutron powder diffraction (NPD) and pair-distribution-function (PDF) analysis without human intervention. Deployed at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS), the agent orchestrates established refinement software through a hierarchical “Reasoning + Acting” framework. Its core innovation, Agentic Context Operation (ACO), maintains a coherent ‘working memory’ of file paths, intermediate results, and domain-specific rules across entire processing steps, even when the underlying large language model undergoes context compression. Across reference materials (Si, CsAgTe and Bi2MoO6), the agent refined structural parameters statistically indistinguishable from expert-derived solutions, while requiring markedly fewer iterative cycles. In an exhaustive 18-run factorial ablation study on two high-entropy alloys, we systematically evaluated the MemoWrite and CoreSkillWrite in ACO mechanisms with and without 50k-token context compression, quantifying the necessity of each component. Memo improved both mean composite performance and repeatability even without compression (+ 20.2% and + 11.3%, respectively). Under compression, Memo improved these metrics by + 10.7% and + 17.0%, and retaining CoreSkill provided a further + 12.5% and + 6.6% improvement, yielding a mean composite score of 0.9316 and repeatability stability of 0.9905 for full ACO. The agent is integrated with a permission-controlled CSNS data interface, enabling secure, on-demand analysis of user-proprietary data with automatic archiving.
evidence_items.title: An agentic AI neutron scattering data scientist at the China Spallation Neutron Source

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis relies on computational methods that shape biological conclusions. Developing new methods requires identifying computational operations that address problem constraints to produce intended effects. Here we investigate coordinated agents that extract methodological reasoning from full-text literature and reuse it as prior knowledge for method hypothesis generation. We instantiate this approach as scHypothesizer, a knowledge-grounded agentic framework that uses Mechanism-centered Generation (MCG) to formulate hypotheses from literature-derived Research Primitive Knowledge Graphs (RPKGs) and subjects them to early empirical assessment. We show that coordinated agents recover source-supported reasoning and that full-text RPKGs preserve more complete reasoning than abstract-only representations. In time-filtered retrospective evaluation of 2,429 Problems, MCG achieved the best ranking performance among compared retrieval methods, with a query-macro AUROC of 0.783 and Hit@10 of 69.1%. Finally, scHypothesizer supported early empirical assessment of four researcher-approved hypotheses, providing informative evidence regarding intended Effects, the settings in which they hold, and associated limitations. Together, these results suggest that coordinated agents can make methodological reasoning from prior studies reusable as source-traceable knowledge for generating new method hypotheses and informing their early empirical assessment.
evidence_items.title: A Knowledge-grounded Agentic Framework for Single-cell RNA Sequencing Method Hypothesis Generation

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the paper "Inferring Gender from Author Names with Local LLMs: A Multi-Model Evaluation" (Journal of Informetrics, 2026). It contains 194,528 first name–country pairs derived from Wikidata, along with gender predictions (Man / Woman / Unknown) produced by 25 open-weight large language models run locally via Ollama, ranging from 270M to 70B parameters. The ground truth is based on the gender distribution of real people registered in Wikidata for each name and country of origin. The dataset includes: (1) the ground-truth reference file with name, country, and sex; (2) the Wikidata source file with gender probability and frequency statistics; (3) one prediction file per model (25 total); and (4) Python scripts to reproduce the evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1-score) and all figures reported in the paper. Data are released under CC BY 4.0; code under Apache 2.0

evidence_items.summary: Concurrent defects in rotating components produce overlapping vibration components, complicating the recognition of defect combinations absent from training. We formulate this task as compositional multi-label learning and propose a compositional evidence-grounded framework (CEG-LLM). The model uses a frozen large language model as a sequence encoder, with trainable low-rank adapters and four sigmoid defect outputs. Continuous waveform tokens and nominal characteristic-order descriptors represent the signal, while a four-node composition graph conditions label-wise attention. Spectral alignment and compositional regularization guide training, and a fixed template links predictions to structured signal records. On one dataset collected from a rotating component at 1500 rpm, CEG-LLM achieves an observed-state macro-F1 of 0.941. Corresponding values are 0.922 for a one-dimensional vision Transformer (ViT), 0.912 for a signal-to-text language encoder, and 0.900 for a convolutional neural network (CNN). Mean exact match across six withheld defect pairs is 0.767, and macro-F1 at −3 dB is 0.819. A top-token versus random-mask deletion contrast of 0.207 indicates sensitivity to the selected representation under that intervention. These results assess recognition of unseen defect combinations and representation sensitivity within the evaluated operating condition.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Label Learning with a Large Language Model for Compound Defect Detection in Rotating Components

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Radiation Therapy (RT) scheduling requires coordination of clinical constraints and operational objectives. Large language models (LLMs) may provide a natural‐language interface for generating candidate schedules. Purpose To evaluate the feasibility of using an existing LLM to generate RT patient schedules under clinical and operational constraints through simulation and retrospective clinical comparison. Methods A one‐year, three‐linear‐accelerator (LINAC) simulation included 1400 new patients across 12 treatment categories modeled after clinical practice. Structured prompts supplied ChatGPT with patient data, the current schedule state, clinical rules, and scenario‐specific objectives. Performance was evaluated across scenarios addressing weekly treatment‐time consistency, LINAC continuity, gap‐constrained temporal relaxation, and infeasible request handling. LLM‐generated schedules were benchmarked against heuristic and CP‐SAT schedules under two objective settings. A six‐week retrospective comparison evaluated 2043 appointments against a clinical schedule. Results The LLM‐generated schedules satisfied the predefined feasibility rules in all evaluated scenarios. Across scenarios, 98.6%–98.8% of evaluated fractions remained within the preferred treatment‐time window. Adding a LINAC‐continuity objective reduced the LINAC switch rate from 52.4 2.6% to 9.4 0.6%, and gap‐constrained temporal relaxation reduced daily gap to 47.1 8.5 min and Friday gap to 89.2 18.4 min while maintaining low overtime. In infeasible request tests, the framework identified predefined constraint violations and returned interpretable corrective suggestions. The optimization benchmarks also generated feasible schedules, but their results showed strong objective‐weight trade‐offs.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating a large language model for radiotherapy patient scheduling under realistic clinical and operational constraints: A feasibility study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Gold exploration is an evidence-intensive spatial decision problem in which geological structures, host lithologies, alteration assemblages, geochemical anomalies, geophysical responses, and remote-sensing observations must be interpreted jointly across heterogeneous spatial scales. Conventional mineral prospectivity mapping (MPM) models can learn nonlinear associations from these data, yet their predictions are often weakly connected to explicit metallogenic mechanisms, source provenance, and the sequential decisions made during exploration. Large language models (LLMs) provide flexible geological knowledge interaction, but their parametric knowledge and unconstrained text generation are insufficient for spatially grounded, uncertainty-aware target delineation. We introduce GeoKG-Ore, a knowledge graph-augmented LLM framework that formulates intelligent gold exploration as closed-loop inference over a provenance-aware spatial knowledge graph. Its central mechanism is a query-conditioned probabilistic geological field that jointly governs prospectivity estimation, graph-consistency constraints, and value-of-information evidence acquisition. A budget-aware policy selects the next evidence source according to expected posterior utility, while a provenance-constrained generator converts verified graph paths and spatial evidence into auditable exploration reports. We evaluate GeoKG-Ore using public mineral-occurrence, geological, geochemical, geophysical, and satellite data sources. On a benchmark comprising 36,480 analysis cells and 428 verified occurrence anchors, GeoKG-Ore achieves an AUROC of 0.913, an AUPRC of 0.612, and a recall of 0.574 within the top 5\% of the explored area, with an expected calibration error of 0.038. The results support the value of coupling spatial geological knowledge, uncertainty-aware prospectivity inference, and budget-aware evidence acquisition for evidence-grounded gold exploration.
evidence_items.title: GeoKG-Ore: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Large Language Models for Intelligent Gold Exploration

evidence_items.summary: Elevator fault diagnosis is a safety-critical problem that requires capabilities beyond isolated fault classification, including knowledge grounding and structured reasoning for maintenance support. In this work, we present a benchmark for elevator fault diagnosis and organize evaluation into three complementary task groups: (A) sensor-based fault detection and classification, (B) taxonomy-grounded fault classification and cause identification, and (C) reasoning with incomplete or constrained information. To enable reproducible comparison across heterogeneous model families, we standardize task definitions, input/output formats, and scoring protocols and report component-level predictive metrics. Experiments across representative language models show task-dependent performance: higher performance on one task does not necessarily transfer to another. The benchmark is a reproducible testbed for studying diagnostic-assistance methods, not a validation of safe operational deployment.
evidence_items.title: A benchmark for elevator fault diagnosis: Multi-level tasks from perception to diagnostic reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Remaining useful life (RUL) models are evaluated mainly on clean sensor data, whereas deployed monitoring systems lose channels and receive plausible but erroneous values when a sensor freezes, drifts, becomes noisy or spikes. Nine model families were evaluated on the four Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation (C-MAPSS) subsets, and five of them on PHM08, under a deterministic protocol of 24 corruption scenarios, one fault family withheld from training and the clean condition. The root mean square error (RMSE) increased on average by up to 24% under single-sensor drift and by 49–121% under unseen spikes. The robustness of a gated recurrent encoder was traced to the training regime. The coverage of conformalised 90% prediction intervals fell to 70–82% under spikes while the mean interval width of the deep models changed by less than 3%. Since missing entries were tolerated far better than spiked or drifting ones, a detect-then-mask repair was developed that masks entries flagged by clean-data statistics. Applied to 360 saved C-MAPSS checkpoints without retraining, it reduced RMSE under unseen spikes by 30% and under strong drift by 26% at a clean-data cost of 0.04 cycles, and with Mondrian recalibration it restored the coverage under spikes to 89%.
evidence_items.title: Silent Sensor Faults in Remaining Useful Life Prediction: A Robustness Benchmark, Uncertainty Audit and Model-Agnostic Input Repair

evidence_items.summary: Convolutional recurrent networks are widely reported as being able to forecast process temperature in machining accurately. Many such evaluations, however, split overlapping sliding windows at random, which lets near-duplicate samples cross the train–test boundary. We re-examine process temperature forecasting and soft sensing on the AI4I 2020 benchmark under a leakage-controlled protocol: a chronological split with a purge gap, training-only scaling, five seeds, block-bootstrap confidence intervals and Diebold–Mariano tests with an autocorrelation-robust variance. LSTM, GRU, CNN-LSTM and an attention-augmented CNN-LSTM are compared with persistence, linear, random forest and multilayer-perceptron baselines that receive the same ten-record window. Under a random split the attention model reaches R2=0.899±0.006; under the chronological split it falls to 0.305±0.089. Rolling-origin cross-validation, a purge-gap sweep, a factorial ablation and sensitivity analyses support this picture. In soft sensing, the error is dominated by a drifting process–air temperature offset that the machine signals in this benchmark do not observe, and refitting on recent data matters more than architecture. When lagged process temperature is available, persistence (MAE 0.054 K) is not beaten at horizons of 1–30 records, and convolutional and attention stages add no benefit while costing up to 2.4 times the training time of a plain LSTM. On this benchmark, the evaluation protocol changed the conclusions more than did the choice of architecture. Claimed gains of deep sequence models for machine monitoring should therefore be reported against persistence and information-matched baselines under a time-ordered split.
evidence_items.title: Leakage-Controlled Evaluation of CNN-LSTM Models for Process Temperature Forecasting and Soft Sensing in Machining: Evidence from the AI4I 2020 Benchmark

organizations: Boston Children's Hospital; Harvard Medical School
evidence_items.summary: Background Misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. Methods Retrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by an LLM agent, Dr CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). Findings The median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, the LLM agent and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine learning systems are increasingly required to be multi-layered for software engineering validation protocols, and multiple checks are imposed instead of just one. Many important failure modes, such as deep class imbalance, poor probability calibration, ungrounded execution, and ”attributional” issues, come to a head in low-level deployments, such as automated code generation, credit underwriting, and clinical triage, where failures can be devastating. In clinical triage, credit underwriting, and the automated generation of code situations that are of a high stakes regularly show up critical failure modes such as severe class imbalance, poor probability calibration, unfaithful attribution, and ungrounded execution, for which standard k-fold cross-validation and regularized baselines are entirely inadequate. By combining the findings from 41 empirical studies, this review identifies three main levels of architecture: data leakage prevention and baseline benchmarking (Level 1), post-hoc interpretability audits and glass-box comparisons (Level 2), and distribution-free uncertainty quantification (Level 3). It is particularly important to note that a meta-analysis of 297 financial machine learning papers reveals a general disregard for diagnosis; only 7.1% of the papers examined included Remove and Retrain (ROAR) benchmarks for testing the faithfulness of the explanations, whereas 93.9% used TreeSHAP for feature attribution. The existence of multi-tier verification frameworks is especially important in order to prevent silent failure modes in safetycritical software systems, as these findings demonstrate. Class-conditional Mondrian conformal calibration answers the Minority Coverage Collapse Theorem, recovering +61.7 percentage points of minority coverage (p < 10 −80 ), and pairs with conformalized quantile regression and cost-optimal selective human deferral (θ ∗ = ch/CFN).
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning Validation Pipelines: From Tabular Benchmarking to Conformal Calibration and Execution-Grounded Agentic Testing

evidence_items.summary: Reliable evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) and medical vision-language models (Medical-VLMs) requires calibrated confidence, particularly under realistic clinical conditions. However, existing efforts mainly focused on improving accuracy, leaving calibration in the medical domain underexplored. To this end, we propose MVC-Bench, a calibration-centric benchmark for medical image classification with VLMs and Medical-VLMs. MVC-Bench assesses the calibration across three axes: (i) robustness to modality, backbone, and domain shift (ii) effectiveness of calibration strategies and prompt-tuning methods (iii) stability under prompt-template and random-seed variations. The benchmark covers eight different backbones, three medical modalities, including fundus imaging, histopathology, and chest X-ray under in-domain and domain shift settings. It compares post-hoc calibration, train-time calibration, and zero-shot inference methods, together with six prompt-tuning methods. Across more than 1638 controlled experiments, we report accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as primary metrics, and further report results with complementary calibration measures, including Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) and Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE). We further investigate the underlying causes of miscalibration in VLMs and Medical-VLMs and propose a simple train-time calibration method, Multi-Class Margin (MCM) regularization, which achieves lowest ECE on 10 out of 12 settings in in-domain and remains competitive under domain shifts. Collectively, MVC-Bench provides a structured evaluation framework and actionable guidance for improving calibration in safety-critical medical workflows.
evidence_items.title: MVC-Bench: Benchmarking Calibration of Medical Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Instruction-based video editing (IVE) offers diverse applications, yet evaluating editing models remains challenging. Existing benchmarks suffer from two key limitations: narrow task coverage inherited from image editing that overlooks video-specific dimensions, and metrics that inadequately capture instruction fidelity, allowing visually plausible but incorrect edits to receive high scores. To address these limitations, we introduce OmniEdit-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark covering spatial, temporal, audio, and reference-based editing. It distinguishes between explicit and implicit instructions and incorporates reasoning-based scenarios to reflect real-world editing requirements. We further propose an evaluation framework that assesses accuracy, preservation, realism, and consistency using both human judges and a state-of-the-art vision-language model (VLM). An accuracy-aware penalty mechanism conditions the other three scores on accuracy, prioritizing instruction fidelity and penalizing plausible but incorrect edits. Experiments on prominent open-source and commercial IVE models reveal substantial room for improvement. OmniEdit-Bench provides a structured testbed for identifying model limitations and advancing instruction-based video editing. Project page: https://omniedit-bench.github.io.
evidence_items.title: OmniEdit-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Instruction-based Video Editing

evidence_items.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as an unstructured set of primitives optimized at a single scale, offering no native support for progressive delivery to heterogeneous devices. Existing scalable approaches organize these primitives into independent quality layers or spatial hierarchies. However, maintaining separate splat representations across scales introduces redundancy, while independent layers have limited ability to correct coarse geometry as finer detail arrives. We present LiftGS, a multiresolution representation that organizes a scene into a coarse Gaussian set and a tree of refinements. Each refinement replaces one coarse Gaussian with two finer children whose attributes are learned relative to their parent. Inspired by wavelet lifting, we encode these changes using a shared detail vector and per-attribute factors that allow the two children to differ asymmetrically from the parent. A client first receives the coarse set, then reconstructs and substitutes children as refinement data arrives. This construction reuses previously transmitted attributes to encode finer detail and removes replaced parents from the active rendering set, reducing both refinement payload and rendering memory. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets show LiftGS cuts splat redundancy from over 65% to under 25%, reduces transmission payload and GPU memory by up to 2.4x and 5.5x over state-of-the-art scalable-3DGS baselines, achieves smooth quality transitions in simulated progressive delivery, and compresses a further 8.7x with standard coding at negligible quality loss. Project website: https://yuang-ian.github.io/liftgs/
evidence_items.title: Lifting 3D Gaussians: A Wavelet Multiresolution Representation for Scalable Gaussian Splatting Streaming

evidence_items.summary: We present RPC-GS, the first Gaussian Splatting framework for satellite imagery that operates natively with Rational Polynomial Camera (RPC) models. The RPC model is the de facto standard for representing the complex imaging geometry of modern pushbroom satellite sensors. To simplify rendering, prior satellite Gaussian Splatting methods replace the RPC model with perspective or affine camera approximations, leading to geometric errors during reconstruction. RPC-GS avoids these approximations by projecting Gaussian means and covariances directly through the RPC model during the splatting process. We embed the RPC model in a chain of carefully selected geo-coordinate transformations representing a mapping from splatting-suitable scene coordinates to image coordinates. To map the Gaussian covariance matrices, we derive a numerically robust Jacobian-based covariance projection for the (partially nonlinear) coordinate transformations. Since RPCs lack an explicit notion of camera depth, we integrate a metric ray-based depth formulation. We benchmark RPC, perspective, and affine camera models in a unified framework, with our native RPC renderer achieving the lowest reconstruction error on leading satellite benchmark datasets, improving mean altitude error over perspective and affine approximations by 34.3% and 13.5% on DFC2019, and by 5.0% and 1.2% on IARPA2016. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/wagnva/RPC-GS.
evidence_items.title: RPC-GS: Gaussian Splatting with native RPC Rendering for Satellite Imagery

evidence_items.summary: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.
evidence_items.title: M3OPD-Reasoner: An Open Recipe for Post-Training Multimodal Reasoning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.
evidence_items.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Many studies on automated respiratory sound classification report near-perfect accuracy. In most of these studies, respiratory cycles are split randomly into training and test sets, so cycles of the same patient can be found in both sets. This patient-level data leakage makes the reported results higher than the real performance. In this study, we show this problem on the ICBHI 2017 dataset and build a leakage-free benchmark. Methods: We compare TabPFN-3, a pretrained tabular foundation model that predicts by in-context learning without task-specific gradient updates, with eight standard machine learning classifiers in a three-stage framework. Results: When the cycle-level split was replaced by a patient-level split (a stratified five-fold split repeated three times, 15 test folds, with every class present in every test fold), the accuracy of TabPFN-3 decreased from 0.9943 to 0.8722, the macro-F1 from 0.9807 to 0.5010 and the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) from 0.9805 to 0.5788. Nadeau–Bengio-corrected t-tests with Holm adjustment over the 15 folds showed that TabPFN-3 had a significantly higher MCC than all eight baselines. SHAP analysis showed that the first MFCC coefficient, the spectral bandwidth and the RMS energy contributed most to the predictions. We also distilled TabPFN-3 into small student models. The best student, a small transformer (276.3 KB), reached an MCC of 0.5140; its MCC difference from the teacher was not significant after Holm correction, but an equivalence test did not show equivalence and its macro-F1 was significantly lower. A shallow distilled decision tree gave readable rules, mainly for COPD and healthy recordings. Conclusions: Performance on several minority diseases remains low, so the models are not ready for clinical use, and the results should be seen as a realistic baseline for future work.
evidence_items.title: Exposing Patient-Level Data Leakage in Respiratory Sound Classification: A Leakage-Free Benchmark Leveraging Transformer-Based TabPFN-3 and Knowledge Distillation

evidence_items.title: MYSTERIOUS EASTERN CULTURE QUANTUM ENTANGLEMENT AND VOLITIONAL CORRELATION TESTS FAMILY 20  ·  F096–F100  ·  Scientific Technical Notebook v1.0 讓古老的謎題保有詩意,讓未來的科學保有謙遜;讓每一個尚未解開的問題,都有機會成為下一個文明的起點。 Let ancient mysteries retain their poetry, and future science its humility; let every unanswered question become a possible beginning for the next civilization. 33 × STARLI  |  White Rainbow Epoch Prospective · Nonclinical · Falsifiable · Recomputable. All numerical examples are synthetic. No clinical or volitional-entanglement claim is established. F096 · Physical Feasibility of Volition-Related Quantum Entanglement Hypotheses at the Limit F097 · Nonlocal Neural Correlations and Common-Cause Exclusion at the Limit F098 · Entanglement Witnesses and Identifiability in Neural Measurements at the Limit F099 · Distant Volitional Synchrony Claims and Information-Leakage Blinding at the Limit F100 · Quantum Entanglement Versus Classical Correlation in Volitional Research at the Limit   Scientific position and cultural inheritance Five evidence identities F096 asks whether a specified physical joint state and measurement path are even feasible. F097 compares neural associations against common-cause alternatives. F098 requires a physically defined witness; F099 investigates concealed-target identification; F100 tests classical predictive residuals. These outputs have different units and logical meanings. A likelihood ratio does not have the interpretation of an operator expectation or an accuracy contrast. A negative result at one necessary link cannot be paid for by a high score elsewhere. The family is integrated by traceable interfaces, not by a civilization index. Entanglement is a property of specified subsystems A nonseparable density operator is not defined by a narrative about connectedness. The tensor partition, physical preparation and observation operators establish the question. Classical mixtures can produce striking correlations. Begin with reference qubits in a controlled bench or simulation; verify independent preparation and record losses, phase, basis, source identity and uncertainty. Do not extrapolate a verified laboratory entangled state to neural tissue without an independently validated transduction and state model. Bell tests and the locality boundary The CHSH inequality constrains a class of local hidden-variable models under specified assumptions. Hensen and colleagues used independently controlled electron spins in diamond; this is not a demonstration in human brains. The experiment must specify the settings, admissible trials, event ordering and outcome distribution. Analyze the actual four setting-conditioned correlations, not an ordinary Pearson coefficient from two EEG traces. Even a valid Bell violation does not provide controllable faster-than-light signalling. Ordinary correlation deserves the strongest defense A shared environment, clock, stimulus schedule or physiological rhythm can create cross-site association. F097 makes this ordinary explanation a serious predictive model rather than a weak nuisance adjustment. Measure independent reference channels, precommit preprocessing, retain dyad-level units and fit common-driver alternatives on training records only. A residual unexplained by measured covariates is uncertainty, not a unique indication of nonlocal causation. An operator is not a metaphor F098 starts from a concrete witness, such as the Bell-projector witness W=I/2-P. Negative expectation certifies entanglement for a trusted two-qubit measurement with established assumptions. The blueprint leaves the witness units unspecified. This edition uses a dimensionless normalized operator and requires an explicit mapping for any physical readout; no EEG amplitude is silently promoted to that operator. A witness can miss some entangled states. Failure of a particular witness is not universal separability unless the chosen test is complete for that state family. Independent settings and trial accounting Detection loss, setting prediction and memory across trials can bias certification. A physically valid source is not sufficient if the statistical experiment changes which events count. Publish setting-conditioned counts and all registered event statuses. Check calibration and confidence intervals on reference systems, and choose sequential inference consistent with the design. A failed trial-accounting audit vetoes a strong physical attribution even if the plotted statistic looks impressive. Distance is not isolation Distant volitional synchrony is a behavioral claim until a physical mechanism has independently been identified. A target bit could travel through an ordinary sensory, digital or procedural channel. Seal responses before target disclosure; separate target generation from local event timing and audit ordinary pathways using dummy records rather than participant data. Bound ordinary leakage, and publish uncertainty or abstain when isolation cannot be certified. Qigong and Xianggong as cultural inheritance Qigong and Xianggong may motivate research questions about breath, movement, attention, expectation and reported experience. Their descriptive vocabulary need not be erased to pursue an experiment. Where a consented nonclinical practice protocol is later proposed, preserve participant reports and compare independently scheduled or matched sham contexts. Odor, breathing and instruction are ordinary variables. No traditional concept is assumed to be a quantum state, a force or a mechanism of information transfer. Daoist humility and the discipline of refusal Relational change and restraint can inspire a method that leaves room for uncertainty. They are philosophical analogies rather than derivations of Bell inequalities. A decision ledger records the distinction between a measured result, an unresolved alternative, a failed calibration and a claim withdrawn after an adversarial test. A cultural idea can retain its poetry even when a particular proposed physical interpretation fails. A classical competitor is a positive research object F100 allows dynamic latent-factor models, nonlinear common causes and ordinary sensors to explain the evidence. A residual measures the adequacy of one specified model on a specified dataset. Use matched acquisition and fitting resources, a frozen scoring rule, held-out dyads and proper uncertainty. Compare prediction and calibration, not rhetoric. The benchmark can favor the classical model without implying that quantum mechanics is false.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains 188,857 unlabeled Sentinel-2 RGB image patches of tropical coral reefs and shallow coastal waters. It was built for continued self-supervised pretraining (domain adaptation) of vision foundation models for coastal and shallow-water remote sensing. This corpus was used to adapt DINOv3 ViT-B/16 to shallow coastal environments in the paper "On the Transferability of Earth Observation Foundation Models to Coastal Environments" (2nd Workshop on Advances in Representation Learning for Earth Observation, NeurIPS 2026). Code, the adapted encoder, and documentation: https://github.com/DHI/CoastalEOFoundationModels Overview - Patches: 188,857 retained after quality filtering (out of 200,530 scanned) - Locations: 19,768 distinct patch footprints, each imaged on 1–14 dates (mean 9.6) - Coverage: 65 MGRS tiles in 30 UTM zones, 24.2°S to 25.3°N. Regions include Belize and the Caribbean, the Red Sea, Southeast Asia, the Great Barrier Reef, and other tropical reef areas. - Period: 2017–2025 - Source: Sentinel-2 Level-2A, bands B4/B3/B2 (true-color RGB) - Format: GeoTIFF, 224 × 224 px, 3 bands, uint8 (8-bit stretched), 10 m ground sampling distance (2.24 km per patch side) - Labels: none. Each patch has metadata: tile, acquisition date, location index, and coordinates. Files - Patch archives: Once extracted, each tile folder holds patches named <TILE> <YYYYMMDD> <location index>.tif. Patches with the same location index share the same footprint. - manifest.csv: one row per retained patch; this is the training index. Columns: path, tile, date, year, month, season (hemisphere-aware), lon and lat (patch center, WGS84), location index, the quality statistics used for filtering, and per-band means. - manifest rejected.csv: one row per rejected patch, with the reason for rejection. - manifest stats.json: vocabularies, per-tile counts, normalization statistics, and filter settings.

It explores how to address the "Data Wall" and Internet exhaustion—where human public text data is running out—by enabling massive synthetic data generation and AlphaZero-style self-play reasoning while preventing model collapse caused by "synthetic inbreeding" (progressive degradation from… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/LinteAI/linteai-data-wall-synthetic-collapse.

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or vision-language metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVSCORE addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. A Significance-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing a timestamp- and evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVSCORE outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing highly accurate and interpretable feedback.
evidence_items.title: FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: NexSight: Verifiable Tasks for Fine-Grained Agentic Long-Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.
evidence_items.title: From Repositories to Training Environments: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding Agents with Environment Evolution Loop

evidence_items.summary: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.
evidence_items.title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications

evidence_items.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.
evidence_items.title: Regularized Score Centering

evidence_items.summary: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) lets the model act on what it sees by invoking external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporating returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Answering: Learning to Speak First and Act in Streaming Video

evidence_items.summary: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
evidence_items.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs

evidence_items.summary: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation (p=0.003).
evidence_items.title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic benchmarks that compare machine learning methods under realistic conditions, particularly sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode. Most existing studies rely on small, private datasets with inconsistent protocols, rendering results non-comparable and slowing progress. We introduce Breath-Dx, the first comprehensive benchmark of time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening. Our work leverages the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset, the largest public clinical eNose collection to date, comprising 1,234 patients across nine diagnostic groups, each providing a 17-channel multivariate time series with explicit temporal train/test splits that account for sensor drift. We systematically evaluate 10 methods spanning four families: feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based, and time series architectures. All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation (0.05-0.12 AUC drop compared to random cross-validation), confirming that drift embeds a strong temporal signal. Under this realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance. Recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance across diseases, while specialized time series methods achieve the highest peak results. Demographic confounders matter: breath signals provide independent diagnostic value for some conditions but add little beyond age for others. We release the S-OH dataset, all temporal splits, evaluation protocols, and code to enable reproducible research and accelerate progress in clinical breathomics.
evidence_items.title: Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose

evidence_items.summary: Linked dataset and Python code for a species-level anatomical and morphometric analysis of aircraft damage in bird strikes. The package contains 88,619 FAA National Wildlife Strike Database records (2016–2025) linked to AVONET species-level morphometric traits (535 species), the FAA–AviList–AVONET species crosswalk, analysis scripts (logistic regression models, species- and family-grouped cross-validation, principal component analysis of body size and shape, sensitivity analyses) and result files. See README.md for details. Version 2 adds a cluster bootstrap with full model refitting (1,000 replicates) for all reported ΔAUC intervals (script 10 refit bootstrap all.py).

evidence_items.summary: Journeyman grades how an agent worked, not whether it passed. It drops an agent into eight small simulated jobs — diagnose a crashed service, assay an alloy at a bench, walk a fogged maze, pick up a night shift from a note that lies — and scores the walk on ten axes: did it keep hitting a wall that had already answered, did it stop when the work's object was served or when the budget ran out, could it name what it could not reach and price it, did it repeat a planted false story as fact. Nothing touches real files; every world is simulated and seed-rebuilt, so a claimed exit never reached is caught by arithmetic. What is unusual is not the grading — it is who is allowed to grade. Calibrating an LLM judge before trusting it is standard advice; almost nobody ships the labels to do it with. Three things follow from taking it literally. The calibration set is inside the package: 82 cases across seven axes, labelled by a three-family council in a blind round and an anonymous evidence-quoted second round, distilled from real agent records rather than synthetic vignettes. A judge that has not passed it cannot score — journeyman qualify grants or refuses a badge, and an unqualified run is stamped NOT COMPARABLE. And the judges that failed are published by name, beside the ones that passed. Two scoring layers, and the boundary between them is enforced. Facts are counted programmatically from the record; the questions no counter can answer go to a pluggable judge, one call per rubric item, with the verdict echoed from a fixed label set. Moving a judgement into a deterministic counter to save a call is a standing prohibition, not a preference. The record of being wrong is shipped with it. The first calibration set taught a lesson that the second retracted: under the earlier questions no judge outside one family read one axis at threshold, and that looked like a finding about judging skill. Under the revised definition every judge screened passes it.
evidence_items.title: Journeyman: a process-quality benchmark for LLM agents

evidence_items.summary: Vision-Language Models increasingly rely on textual reasoning to solve advanced multimodal tasks. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm faces two fundamental limitations. First, relying on textual reasoning alone can limit perceptual ability in vision-centric questions, where accurate answers depend on interpreting task-relevant visual evidence. Second, applying textual reasoning uniformly across inputs overlooks question-dependent variation in both reasoning modality and depth, often producing verbose and unnecessary traces when little logical inference is required. To this end, we propose Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning (AVTR), which introduces visual imagination as a complementary reasoning modality to textual thinking, enabling the model to revisit its visual observations and distill the salient evidence through generative visual reflection. Furthermore, we formulate reasoning-modality selection as a learned routing problem, allowing a single policy to adaptively harness the complementary strengths of visual reflection and textual reasoning in response to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Across 16 benchmarks, AVTR improves the average score by 4.5 points over Qwen3.5 baseline, while reducing inference latency by 33\%. It also scales effectively into a smaller size backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.
evidence_items.title: AVTR: Adaptive Multimodal Reasoning with Visual Imagination

evidence_items.summary: Supporting visual recovery and semantic interpretation within the same communication framework remains difficult when channel quality deteriorates. To address this issue, this paper proposes a large language model (LLM)-guided channel-aware semantic communication framework that jointly supports these two tasks through decoupled transmission streams. An LLM-based channel-aware encoder jointly processes image features and a textual prompt describing the current channel condition. This design allows the semantic representation to adapt to different signal-to-noise ratio levels while retaining an independent reconstruction pathway. A lightweight learnable masking mechanism is also incorporated to scramble the transmitted latent features. The ablation results indicate that this mechanism introduces only a limited impact on reconstruction performance. Evaluation under additive white Gaussian noise shows that the proposed design remains effective across the tested channel conditions. In particular, the framework achieves classification accuracies of 90.58% and 88.23% at 0 dB on the CIFAR-10 and Intel image classification datasets, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Large language model-guided channel-aware semantic communication

organizations: School of Mechanical Engineering, Hangzhou Dianzi University, Hangzhou 310018, China
evidence_items.summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have accelerated the real-world deployment of embodied intelligent robots, supporting intuitive human–robot interaction without specialized robotics expertise. However, few systematic assessments examine how well LLMs translate natural-language route instructions into executable robot command sequences, particularly for non-English instructions and across deployment-relevant model classes. In this paper, a Chinese route-instruction corpus was constructed, which comprised 212 instructions collected from six native speakers across 50 procedurally generated town maps. Each was annotated with a ground-truth command sequence verified by simulation to reach its goal, and a 100% performance ceiling was established. Using this corpus, 12 LLMs spanning three capability tiers—cloud proprietary models, mid-sized open-weight models, and small open-weight models—were evaluated under three system prompts differing only in the number of worked examples (zero, one, and three). Open-weight models in the 3–9B range reached at most 9.2% of goals, while proprietary cloud models reached 80.0%, a substantial gap that increasing the number of worked examples did not measurably narrow. A paired analysis across the three prompt conditions detected no reliable effect of demonstration count: pooled path reach rose modestly from 25.0% under zero-shot prompting to 27.2% with one example and 27.7% with three examples (three versus zero examples: odds ratio: 1.15; 95% CI: 0.98–1.34). None of these differences was significant after multiple-comparison correction (Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.247). Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on 126 examples raised mid-sized open-weight models to 27.7–35.4%, and the gain spanned both output-format compliance and route competence.
evidence_items.title: A Model-Class Comparison of Large Language Models for Translating Chinese Route Instructions into Robot Command Sequences

evidence_items.summary: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS’s pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question–answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22–33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4–22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.
evidence_items.title: Synthesis of Reliable Logic Question Answering Data for Large Language Model with the Aid of Operations Research Program

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) offer promising prospects as biocryoprotectants, yet their discovery remains a great challenge due to the lack of efficient large-scale screening tools. Here, we present a benchmark-optimized, multimodel computational pipeline that integrates property evaluation and structural assessment for high-throughput AFP identification. Through systematic benchmarking on independent testing data set, two optimal strategies were identified: the two-model-based Strategy 8 achieved the highest accuracy of 0.82, while the stricter four-model-based Strategy 18 attained the highest precision of 0.97, making it optimal for initial large-scale screening. Furthermore, this pipeline was applied to screen 153,359 Antarctic krill sequences and discovered 13 novel antifreeze peptides. Dynamic ice shaping assays revealed that four out of 13 peptides significantly inhibited ice crystal growth. Notably, Peptide 10 (SPHSWANTYQQCK) could inhibit ice growth and recrystallization. This study establishes a robust framework for large-scale AFP identification and provides a set of experimentally validated Antarctic krill peptides with strong potential as novel biobased cryoprotectants.
evidence_items.title:
Benchmark-Optimized Pipeline Identifies Experimentally
Validated Antifreeze Peptides in Antarctic Krill

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Introduction Physician assistant (PA) programs need practical ways to recognize early academic difficulty. Existing predictors, including admission metrics and later summative assessments, have mixed reliability or occur too late to support timely intervention. This study examined whether first-semester below-benchmark (below-BM) examinnation counts in foundational courses were associated with Physician Assistant National Certifying Examination (PANCE) outcomes. Methods This retrospective, observational study included graduates from five consecutive cohorts with first-attempt PANCE outcomes (N = 228). Below-benchmark counts were summed across Clinical Medicine, Patient Evaluation, and Anatomy exams. Associations between below-BM count and PANCE, Physician Assistant Clinical Knowledge Rating and Assessment Tool (PACKRAT ® ) 1, PACKRAT ® 2, and End of Curriculum (EOC) scores were examined. Below-BM counts were compared by PANCE outcome, and logistic regression examined the association with PANCE failure. Results Below-benchmark count was significantly and negatively correlated with PANCE (ρ = −0.529, P < .001), PACKRAT ® 1 (ρ = −0.491, P < .001), PACKRAT ® 2 (ρ = −0.518, P < .001), and EOC scores (ρ = −0.452, P < .001). Students who failed the PANCE had higher below-BM counts than students who passed (median 4, interquartile range [IQR] 4 vs. median 1, IQR 2; P < .001). Each additional below-BM score increased the odds of PANCE failure by 32% (odds ratio = 1.32, 95% confidence interval [1.07, 1.63], P = .009). Discussion First-semester below-BM count is a simple, early, and easy-to-monitor measure of academic risk that may help PA programs identify students who need support before high-stakes outcomes, including PANCE.
evidence_items.title: First-Semester Below-Benchmark Examination Performance as an Early Indicator of PANCE Risk

organizations: Faculty of Advanced Science and Technology (FAST), Asian Institute of Technology (AIT), Pathum Thani 12120, Thailand

evidence_items.summary: This study examines whether adding waveform-derived information-theoretic descriptors to Mel-spectrogram inputs offers a measurable benefit for five-class amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) dysarthria speech-status classification. The primary evidence is a study-specific, five-fold recording-level CNN comparison: Mel-only accuracy is 0.926±0.012, while historical fusion accuracy is 0.927±0.008. A distinct CNN fusion verification/reproduction run, with traced propagation of the Mel input and all 17 information-theoretic descriptors, reports accuracy of 0.927±0.010; it does not retrospectively verify the archived historical input tensors. Thus, the available comparisons show only a small numerical change, not a demonstrated general advantage of fusion. Complementary analyses include a direct participant-disjoint CNN comparison, a fixed-duration CNN comparison, and seed, duration, padding, and task-specific controls. In the participant-disjoint comparison, Mel-only and fusion achieve accuracies of 0.820 and 0.823, respectively, whereas under the fixed-duration condition they achieve 0.914 and 0.915. These distinct result series show similarly small numerical differences between Mel-only and fusion under the additional evaluation conditions. They do not establish a matched estimate of the effect of participant overlap or a statistically reliable advantage of feature fusion. Source-code auditing identifies discrepancies between an available implementation and the documented score-producing benchmark, without establishing that leakage occurred in the latter. Missing run-linked records, class imbalance, and the absence of external validation constrain conclusions to the evaluated speech-processing pipelines. Class 4 represents ALS without dysarthria, not early bulbar disease detection.
evidence_items.title: Speech-Based Dysarthria Severity Classification in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A Controlled Deep Learning Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate prediction of protein–ligand binding affinities is fundamental to structure-based drug design, yet existing benchmarks are often limited by outdated structural coverage, uncertain local structural fidelity, and physicochemical or protocol-dependent bias. Here, we present HiFiPL-Bench, a fidelity-first and bias-aware benchmark curated from RCSB PDB and BindingDB through hierarchical filtering, manual electron-density validation, affinity verification, and property-matched decoy generation. Across nine representative scoring functions, HiFiPL-Bench revealed reduced performance in scoring, ranking, and most docking evaluations relative to CASF-2016, whereas a controlled screening-like task using computationally generated property-matched decoys produced model-specific gains and losses that altered relative rankings rather than uniformly lowering performance. Model-specific overlap and deoverlap analyses further showed that documented development-data exposure differed substantially among methods and that deoverlapped sensitivity analyses affected models and evaluation tasks nonuniformly. Together, these findings indicate that performance estimates remain sensitive to starting-structure curation, task-specific preparation, data set composition, decoy design, benchmark protocol, and recoverable development-data exposure. HiFiPL-Bench therefore provides a reusable diagnostic framework for evaluating scoring-function performance in a structurally curated and bias-aware benchmark setting.
evidence_items.title:
HiFiPL-Bench: A
Fidelity-First and Bias-Aware Benchmark
for Diagnosing Protein–Ligand Scoring Functions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Post-quantum cryptography migration can depend on the readiness of shared trust, software, control, and recovery services. We evaluate GridPQC-Graph, a temporal relational estimator coupled to constrained migration planning, in a constructed energy-sector benchmark. Six public power-system cases supply physical topology; deterministic cyber-dependency fixtures, archived primitive timings, and a disclosed stochastic label generator supply the remaining evidence. The benchmark contains 769 assets, 5,242 directed relations, and 110,736 controlled trials. Fifty-three time-indexed features feed calibrated histogram gradient boosting. Training, calibration, unseen-topology testing, and later-epoch testing use disjoint rows. Across 20 seeds, the model attains average precision 0.8884 and Brier score 0.1178 on the held-out 300-bus case. Against a newly calibrated logistic comparator, the corresponding paired differences are 0.00415 and − 0.00244; the logistic comparator has lower expected calibration error. Relation-group substitution measures output sensitivity and local ranking stability, without identifying causal effects. A mixed-integer planner enforces maintenance, criticality, privileged-asset, and prerequisite constraints. Its ten-wave mean exposure retirement is 0.3210, with a consequence proxy of 15.895; readiness-first scheduling trades lower consequence for less retired exposure. Optimizer-matched comparisons separate scoring effects from solver choice. These findings establish conditional benchmark performance, not operational effectiveness, field-disruption probabilities, or safe deployment. Formal stochastic models offer complementary assurance when their transition assumptions and probability bounds are independently validated.
evidence_items.title: Explainable temporal relational learning for constraint-aware PQC migration in a constructed energy-sector benchmark

organizations: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Electricity demand forecasting is harder on grids where supply often falls short, because load shedding changes how demand behaves. This study benchmarks one-hour-ahead forecasting on the national grid of Bangladesh from April 2015 to March 2026, a period in which load shedding rose from less than 1% of hours to 44% of hours in 2022 to 2025. Eleven models were compared under a single leak-free protocol: three naive baselines, two linear models, Random Forest, XGBoost and four deep learning architectures (PatchTST, iTransformer, CNN-BiLSTM and BiGRU). All were scored on the same 14,142 test hours from July 2024 to March 2026, 41% of which had load shedding. PatchTST was the most accurate model, with an RMSE of 203.8 MW and a MAPE of 1.26%. Its RMSE was 34% lower than that of a tuned XGBoost and 58% lower than persistence. Diebold-Mariano tests with autocorrelation-robust variance and paired block-bootstrap intervals confirmed that it was significantly better than every other model. The advantage came mainly from load-shedding hours, where the error of XGBoost rose by 36% while that of every deep learning model changed by about 5% or less. Integrated Gradients and TreeSHAP showed that the transformers used the full weekly demand cycle and the recent shedding history, whereas XGBoost could not predict demand above its training range. BatchNorm improved the transformers but not the recurrent models. Forecasting models for energy-constrained grids should therefore be evaluated separately for hours with and without load shedding.
evidence_items.title: Forecasting Electricity Demand Under Severe Load Shedding: An Explainable and Statistically Validated Deep Learning Benchmark

organizations: Department of Emergency, Shijingshan Teaching Hospital, Capital Medical University
evidence_items.summary: Background Biomarkers may show strong outcome associations without adding information to detailed electronic health record (EHR) models. We developed a reproducible benchmark separating association from incremental value for the lactate-to-albumin ratio (LAR) and troponin in older high-acuity patients, with the aim of locating where marker-specific information remains distinct after an information-rich baseline. Methods From 12,000 records in the official CinC 2012 Sets A, B, and C, we included 1,640 patients aged at least 65 years with computable LAR. First-48-h measurements from 37 raw variables produced a transparent 290-feature baseline. Baseline, LAR-augmented, missingness-aware troponin, integrated, and score-enhanced models used L2-regularized logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting. Set A supported development, Set B validation and recalibration, and Set C locked internal testing. Evaluation combined discrimination, calibration, paired bootstrap ablation, optimism correction, decision curves, permutation importance, and risk concentration. Results Mortality rose from 18.2% in the lowest LAR max quartile to 36.7% in the highest, with 2.60-fold higher odds of death. The association pointed in the same direction across four ICU categories (odds ratios per stratum-specific LAR interquartile range, 1.30–1.76). The score-enhanced random forest achieved the highest Set C AUROC (0.769; 95% CI: 0.729–0.809). Recalibration improved its Brier score from 0.200 to 0.170 and moved calibration-in-the-large from − 0.652 to 0.078, thereby reducing average overprediction. Paired-bootstrap intervals for LAR or troponin augmentation crossed zero, locating an information-saturation boundary after the 290-feature EHR baseline; decision-curve mean net benefits for baseline and LAR-augmented gradient boosting were 0.120 and 0.122. Troponin-tested patients had higher mortality than untested patients (31.6% vs. 23.6%).
evidence_items.title: Separating biomarker association from incremental EHR value: a reproducible LAR and troponin benchmark in older high-acuity patients
