evidence_items.summary: Remote sensing (RS) image understanding has significantly advanced through deep learning and vision-language models, yet most approaches still operate mainly as prediction systems that return class labels with limited explanation of the semantic evidence supporting them. Attribute-based representations offer a more interpretable alternative, describing RS scenes in terms of visible objects, dominant colors and geometric patterns. However, these representations are typically used within offline datasets and benchmarking pipelines rather than in interactive systems that enable users to inspect, query and reuse semantic reasoning. This paper presents GeoRS-Agent, an agentic geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) framework for explainable and attribute-grounded RS scene understanding. A vision–language model reports 38 attributes, a deterministic classifier assigns one of 19 classes from class–attribute profiles, and a language model explains the decision citing only the evidence used; an agentic mode exposes these components as tools. On 301 test images, with Qwen2.5-VL 7B throughout, the pipeline reached 58.1% accuracy, against 71.1% with the class list in the prompt, 77.4% with the knowledge base also in the prompt, and 91.7% with reference attributes; with profiles estimated from the model’s own attributes it reached 75.1% in an exploratory analysis; its difference from the knowledge-in-prompt condition was not statistically significant, while the class decision remained inspectable. Explanations were always consistent with the evidence; tools improved knowledge and contrastive queries but not counterfactual ones.
evidence_items.title: GeoRS-Agent: An Agentic GeoAI Framework for Attribute-Grounded and Explainable Remote Sensing Scene Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Security operations capabilities are commonly distributed across security operations centres (SOCs), security information and event management (SIEM), vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT), security awareness training (SAT), secure software development life-cycle (SDLC) practices, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) controls, and AI security testing. Although enterprise platforms increasingly integrate telemetry, detection, response, cloud and identity capabilities, evidence and workflows across these seven capability areas are not necessarily connected through a shared, auditable operating model. This paper proposes a Unified Agentic Security Operations Platform (UASP), a conceptual architecture for coordinating the seven capabilities through specialist agents, a shared telemetry and evidence substrate, risk-context orchestration, and policy-governed human oversight. The framework specifies six illustrative feedback loops, including VAPT findings informing development and pipeline controls, deployment provenance enriching SOC investigations, security incidents informing targeted awareness interventions, and AI security testing events becoming correlated SIEM/SOC telemetry. It distinguishes the operational roles of the SOC and SIEM, and of secure SDLC and CI/CD, while allowing them to be implemented through coordinated agents. The design uses the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) for event normalization and treats entity, temporal and provenance modelling as a complementary semantic layer. It also defines bounded autonomy, risk-graded approvals, and an evaluation agenda. The paper is a narrative conceptual synthesis of selected standards, research and public vendor materials; it does not report a deployed implementation, original empirical dataset, or measured performance results. Its contribution is therefore a structured architecture and a set of testable design propositions for subsequent implementation and evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Toward a Unified Agentic Security Operations Platform: A Conceptual Architecture for Cross-Domain Cybersecurity Integration

evidence_items.summary: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.
evidence_items.title: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains processed analytical data, computational scripts, dependency-network configurations, model parameters, and numerical outputs supporting the study "Identifying Cascade-Vulnerability Archetypes in Interdependent Infrastructure Systems under Multiple Hazards." The archive contains canonical and alternative dependency networks, model parameterizations, asset-level vulnerability indicators, archetype assignments, and sensitivity and robustness analyses. The outputs are conditional on the adopted modelling assumptions and are not empirically calibrated predictions of infrastructure failure. Certain upstream geospatial provenance information is incomplete. evidence_items.summary: High-numerical-aperture focusing is intrinsically vectorial and becomes particularly complex to describe when light propagates through refractive index discontinuities and multilayer structures, where polarization-dependent transmission, multiple reflections and interference modify the focal field. We present MultiLayerFocus, an open Python-based software toolbox designed to model these effects within a unified numerical environment. The method combines the Debye–Wolf description of high-NA focusing with a coherent transfer-matrix treatment of planar stratified media, allowing the complex electric field to be reconstructed before, inside and after the multilayer. The numerical implementation is independently validated against the semi-analytical Richards–Wolf solution, showing convergence of all three complex Cartesian field components, and is subsequently applied to representative high-NA configurations. The multilayer implementation is further validated through numerical consistency tests on randomly generated stratified configurations, assessing complex reflection and transmission coefficients, electromagnetic boundary conditions, and energy conservation. Simulations across a broad range of commercial microscope objectives show the progressive redistribution of the focal field from transverse to longitudinal components with increasing angular aperture, while also highlighting that nominal numerical aperture alone does not determine the longitudinal-field contribution when different immersion media are considered. Radially polarized illumination produces the expected strong on-axis longitudinal field and provides a case study of the three-dimensional polarization analysis. Dielectric and absorbing multilayers further demonstrate the ability to resolve field evolution across interfaces and within finite layers, including thickness-dependent transmission through metallic films.
evidence_items.title: Dataset of "MultiLayerFocus – a toolbox for vectorial focusing in stratified media"

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the manuscript of the article “Cavity-Mediated Radiative Energy Transfer Enables Stable, Low-Threshold Lasing in Hybrid Quantum Dot-Nanoplatelet Supraparticles” by Cristian Gonzalez, Yun Chang Choi, Gary Chen, Jun Xu, Claire Yejin Kang, Emanuele Marino, Cherie R. Kagan and Christopher B. Murray. The study reports hybrid supraparticles composed of CdSe/ZnS quantum dots and CdSe/CdₓZn₁₋ₓS nanoplatelets. Cavity-mediated energy transfer from broadband-absorbing quantum dots to narrow-emitting nanoplatelets enables stable whispering-gallery-mode lasing with a low threshold of 0.35 mJ cm⁻². The supraparticles retain their optical performance under prolonged exposure to air, water and continuous irradiation. Article DOI: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.5c15222 Published in ACS Nano 2026, 20, 2114–2124. This manuscript is deposited for scholarly and open-research purposes. Copyright is held by the American Chemical Society. The associated research data are deposited separately in a dedicated dataset record. The work was supported in part by the European Research Council through ERC Starting Grant REFINE2LASE, grant agreement No. 101202342.
evidence_items.title: Cavity-Mediated Radiative Energy Transfer Enables Stable, Low-Threshold Lasing in Hybrid Quantum Dot-Nanoplatelet Supraparticles

evidence_items.summary: In modern cloud-native systems ensuring au tonomous and efficient workload orchestration is critical to meeting the latency and performance requirements of future telecommunication ecosystems. The modern cloud paradigm favors the adoption of microservices architectures along with the assurance that they meet the stringent standards of service distribution such as elasticity, high availability and proxim ity awareness. Elasticity ensures that computational resources are efficiently allocated and properly provisioned, while high availability guarantees self-healing and fault-tolerant service delivery. Proximity awareness enables service placement close to end-users, minimizing latency and preventing service level agreement (SLA) violations to support a seamless user experience across distributed infrastructures. In this paper, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) orchestration framework that unifies service provisioning and placement under a single scheduling policy across the cloud-edge continuum (CEC). Our approach enhances traditional DRL with Transformer-based attention modeling, enabling the agent to capture complex spatiotemporal patterns in workload and resource behavior. To ensure reliable decision execution, a hierarchical two-stage action masking mechanism is employed to enforce feasibility constraints and filter high-uncertainty actions based on policy entropy. The framework is deployed and evaluated in a multi node cloud testbed, demonstrating improved SLA compliance, resource efficiency and stability. Our results position the proposed model as a scalable, zero-touch orchestration solution for future cloud-native and distributed computing infrastructures.
evidence_items.title: MIND the Proximity a Transformer-Based RL Scheduler and Placement Optimizer for Cloud-Edge Workloads

evidence_items.summary: Lignocellulosic biomass has increasingly assumed an important role as a renewable feedstock for the production of energy and chemical compounds, representing a sustainable alternative to fossil resources. Among forest biomasses, Eucalyptus globulus stands out due to its abundance and its favorable composition for fractionation. The valorization of this biomass relies on the selective deconstruction of its main polymers — hemicelluloses, cellulose, and lignin — enabling the recovery of purified fractions with potential industrial applications. In this context, the present work evaluated a sequential fractionation process of Eucalyptus globulus wood, combining autohydrolysis, aimed at the selective solubilization of hemicelluloses, with organosolv pulping, intended for lignin removal and the production of cellulose-enriched solids, thus allowing the selective recovery of the main biomass fractions. Autohydrolysis was performed under previously optimized conditions, while the organosolv process employed non-catalyzed ethanol/water mixtures. The effects of autohydrolysis severity, organosolv temperature, and ethanol/water ratio on solid yield, fraction composition, and polymer extraction efficiency were investigated, enabling the evaluation of operational intensification. The chemical characterization of the solids obtained after autohydrolysis revealed cellulose enrichment, with a glucan content of 50.08%, accompanied by a Klason lignin content of 33.54%, confirming the removal of hemicelluloses (acetyl groups, arabinan, and xylan). After the organosolv treatment, a significant increase in the cellulose fraction was observed, reaching a glucan content of 88.92%, evidencing the effective removal of the remaining components, namely hemicelluloses and lignin.
evidence_items.title: Intensificação de Processos de Fracionamento de Biomassa e de Recuperação dos seus Produtos

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Defining transversal competences is only a first step; teachers also need to know how to build lessons that develop several of them at once and how to collect evidence that development has taken place. This article deals with these practical questions for a 4+1C framework in foreign language education, made up of communication, collaboration, critical thinking, creativity and cross-cultural competence. Drawing on sociocultural theory, the interaction approach to second language acquisition, backward design, constructive alignment and task-based language teaching, the study uses a conceptual-analytical design to derive six design principles. It then proposes an assessment scheme that links each competence to evidence, instruments and criteria, and illustrates the principles with a project unit in which upper-intermediate learners prepare a walking tour of their neighbourhood for international visitors. The discussion considers how the components reinforce and sometimes work against each other, notably the pull between convergent evaluation in critical thinking and divergent idea generation in creativity, and the risk that group products hide individual contributions. It warns against turning the framework into a checklist and outlines implications for curriculum, assessment and teacher education. The proposals are presented as a basis for classroom trials and empirical evaluation.
evidence_items.title: DESIGNING AND ASSESSING INTEGRATED 4+1C LEARNING IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE CLASSROOMS: PRINCIPLES, EVIDENCE AND AN ILLUSTRATIVE PROJECT UNIT

evidence_items.summary: Product reviews shape what people buy, yet their credibility is under a fresh threat: large language models (LLMs) can now mass-produce reviews that are fluent, varied and grammatically flawless. Current detectors cope with this only in part. The best-performing published systems lean on transformer models, paid LLM interfaces or reviewer metadata, resources that smaller platforms often lack, whereas lighter classical models were largely designed around older, human-written spam. We compare five recent studies of fake-review detection, looking at their data, labelling, methods, reported accuracy and acknowledged limitations. Two patterns emerge: accuracy tends to rise together with computational cost, and some of the highest accuracies rest on heuristic or weakly supervised labels, which casts doubt on what they actually measure. Drawing on these observations, we propose a lightweight, interpretable pipeline that pairs TF-IDF n gram features with stylometric indicators of machine generated text and compares four classifiers: Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine and Random Forest. The accompanying evaluation protocol is fully specified and includes stratified hold-out and cross validation, cross-generator and cross-domain tests, paraphrase robustness and ablation. Experimental results for the proposed pipeline are not included in this version, and no performance figures are claimed for it. The system is intended as a risk-scoring aid for human moderators, never as proof of AI authorship.
evidence_items.title: Detection of AI-Generated and Deceptive Fake Reviews on E-Commerce Platforms Using Lightweight Machine Learning

evidence_items.summary: This study analyses the malting barley value chain in the Czech Republic, covering all major stages from primary barley production through malting and brewing to the final beer market. The report examines the functional structure of the value chain, including global and national market developments, production trends, trade patterns, governance mechanisms, and the economic performance of key actors. Particular attention is devoted to the strategic importance of spring malting barley, the highly concentrated malting sector, and the role of breweries as the main generators of value added. The analysis combines secondary statistical data, industry reports, company financial statements, and value chain methodologies based on the VCA4D framework. Economic assessments are conducted for representative farm, malting, and brewery archetypes, enabling the evaluation of profitability, value added, and the sector’s contribution to the national economy. The study also investigates market concentration, subsidy dependence, self-sufficiency, export performance, and the impacts of climate change on barley production. The results indicate that the Czech malting barley value chain is strongly export-oriented, with domestic barley production significantly exceeding domestic consumption and substantial exports of both malt and beer. While the sector generates considerable value added and employment, it faces several challenges, including climate-related risks, market concentration in malting, declining beer consumption, and exposure to international commodity market volatility. The study concludes that future competitiveness will depend on innovation, climate resilience, product differentiation, premiumization, and the continued development of export and non-alcoholic beer markets.
evidence_items.title: Value chain analysis of malting barley in the Czech Republic

evidence_items.summary: This dataset was collected from an experimental study investigating the effects of fixed joystick control gain on control behavior, task performance, and human factors in simulated excavator teleoperation. A 3 (control gain: low 0.4, medium 0.7, and high 1.0; between-subjects) × 4 (task type: target positioning, path tracking, obstacle avoidance, and precision manipulation; within-subjects) mixed experimental design was employed. A total of 60 participants were recruited, with 20 participants assigned to each gain condition. The experiment was conducted using a Unity-based excavator simulation platform operated through dual physical joysticks. Task performance measures included completion time, positioning failures, path-tracking root mean square error, collision count, and placement error. Continuous joystick control behavior was characterized using mean input magnitude (MIM), active input ratio (AIR), and direction reversal rate (DRR). Surface electromyography data from the right flexor carpi radialis muscle were also collected, and subjective workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). This dataset supports the investigation of control behavior, task performance, and human factors under different fixed control gain conditions. It may contribute to research on control parameter optimization, human-computer interaction, and ergonomics in excavator teleoperation.
evidence_items.title: Experimental Dataset on Joystick Control Gain, Control Behavior, and Task Performance in Simulated Excavator Teleoperation

evidence_items.summary: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.
evidence_items.title: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential approach to inferring standardized questionnaire responses from qualitative interviews, but their utility for assessing parenting remains unclear. We evaluated six generative LLMs using zero-shot prompting to infer responses to the Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale (MAPS) from interviews with 43 parents. Models inferred responses to 35 MAPS items from two introductory questions about family, parenting roles, and the meaning of caregiving. Performance was evaluated through exact item-response agreement, correlations between inferred and self-reported parenting scores, systematic score differences, and internal consistency. Across models, Fisher-averaged correlations between inferred and self-reported MAPS subscale scores ranged from .320 to .434, with no consistently superior model. Correlations were strongest and most consistent for Warmth, whereas Physical Control showed little correspondence and substantial floor restriction. Across parent–item pairs, 35.5%–44.7% of inferred responses exactly matched parents’ selected response categories. All models assigned systematically lower response categories than parents and rarely selected the highest category; score underestimation was particularly evident for Positive Parenting. Model-derived subscales generally showed internal consistency, although higher internal consistency did not consistently correspond to stronger correlations with parent-reported scores. Exploratory analyses indicated modest similarity in the associations of inferred and self-reported parenting scores with other psychological constructs. Preliminary comparisons also suggested that shorter interview segments substantially reduced computational requirements without clear evidence of poorer performance.
evidence_items.title: How closely do large language model scores from parent interviews match self-reported parenting?

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, accelerated by the growing computational demands of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has led to an unprecedented increase in electricity consumption. As AI developers race to deploy GenAI products, time-to-market pressure drives continuous model training that demands baseload power, often from high-CO 2 emissions sources like natural gas and coal instead of intermittent renewables like wind and solar. Carbon-aware strategies that shift model training in real time to periods or locations with cleaner power on the margin have emerged as a near-term decarbonization lever, but the relative effectiveness of temporal flexibility (pausing model training during high-carbon hours) versus spatial flexibility (migrating workloads to cleaner grid regions) remains poorly understood under real-world constraints. This study evaluates these strategies using 2025 marginal operating CO 2 emissions rate (MOER) data from WattTime across 43 subregions spanning four US grid operators: California Independent System Operator (CAISO), Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), Midcontinent Independent System Operator, and Pennsylvania–Jersey–Maryland (PJM). Using Meta’s LLaMA 3.1 model family as representative workloads, we simulate four scenarios: business-as-usual, reflecting a carbon-informed siting choice with no real-time operational flexibility (S1, BAU); temporal flexibility with varying pause thresholds (S2); ideal spatial flexibility (S3); and spatial flexibility incorporating migration overhead (S4). We find that effective strategies are grid-dependent. In grids with high subregional MOER heterogeneity, spatial flexibility dominates: ERCOT achieves up to 36% emissions reduction via intraday alternation between wind-rich and solar-heavy zones, and the inter-ISO configuration achieves 67.3% reduction, with CAISO and ERCOT absorbing over 80% of training hours.
evidence_items.title: Carbon-aware scheduling of large language model training across multiple US power grid operators: a marginal emissions analysis

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are growing increasingly powerful. Yet, fundamental constraints on the reasoning, memory, and performance of individual models has sparked recent interest in scaling abilities using LLM teams. With growing deployment of LLM teams at scale, there is a need for principled guidelines for when teams help, how many agents to use, and how structure impacts performance. Rather than building these teams through trial-and-error, we propose using distributed systems as a formal foundation for designing and evaluating LLM teams. Under this formal framework, we derive predictions about how task structure and team architecture should shape performance. Empirical evidence supports these predictions: LLM team scaling follows classical distributed computing laws based on the structure of a task, and centralized and decentralized architectures exhibit the asymmetric vulnerabilities predicted by distributed systems theory. These results establish distributed computing as a generative framework that yields testable, quantitative predictions about LLM team behavior and informs the construction of more efficient and capable teams.
evidence_items.title: Language model teams as distributed systems

evidence_items.summary: Catalysis is central to energy conversion and green chemistry, but its development is constrained by fragmented literature data, complex reaction systems, difficult mechanistic identification, and reliance on empirical trial and error. Large language models (LLMs), with capabilities in unstructured text understanding, multisource knowledge integration, reasoning, and tool invocation, have been increasingly applied to literature extraction, characterization analysis, mechanistic hypothesis generation, catalyst recommendation, condition optimization, and automated experimentation. However, catalytic tasks are highly specialized, condition‐dependent, and validation‐intensive, making general‐purpose LLMs insufficient for traceable, verifiable, safe, and controllable research. This review summarizes recent progress in applying LLMs to key catalytic tasks and discusses their reliability requirements. We further propose a catalysis‐oriented vertical LLM framework consisting of “task definition–evidence access–constraint control–model adaptation–validation evaluation–feedback updating.” By integrating evidence‐constrained knowledge extraction, constraint‐aware decision‐making, and feedback‐driven closed‐loop optimization, this framework aims to reduce low‐value trial‐and‐error experiments, unnecessary reagent consumption, energy input, and waste generation, thereby supporting reliable and sustainable catalysis research.
evidence_items.title: Construction of Reliable Vertical Large Language Model Systems for Sustainable Catalysis: From Evidence‐Bound Knowledge Extraction to Closed‐Loop Catalyst Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Aim: Artificial intelligence-based systems are increasingly used for recognizing and assessing skin lesions, yet studies focusing on pregnancy-specific dermatological findings are limited. This study aimed to compare the accuracy of artificial intelligence based large language models in diagnosing pregnancy related dermatological lesions, explaining their etiopathogenesis, and providing clinically appropriate treatment recommendations.Materials and Methods: In this observational study, ten pregnancy-specific dermatological lesions were evaluated using ChatGPT (version 5) and Google Gemini (version 2.5). Each case was presented with an image from Williams Obstetrics, 26th edition, and a standardized patient statement: “I am pregnant. I have a skin lesion like this. What is it, why does it occur, and what should I do for treatment?” Responses were blindly rated by obstetrics and gynecology and dermatology specialists for diagnostic accuracy, etiopathogenesis explanation, and treatment appropriateness, using a five-point Likert scale. Cohen’s kappa was used to assess inter-rater agreement; the Wilcoxon test compared the models; Spearman’s correlation examined score relationships. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.Results: ChatGPT outperformed Gemini in etiopathogenesis explanation (p = 0.002) and treatment recommendations (p = 0.002), with no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy (p = 0.336). ChatGPT generally provided more detailed, applicable responses, whereas Gemini often gave limited or purely directive information. Correlations between criteria were weak and statistically insignificant for both models.Conclusions: ChatGPT was superior to Gemini in etiopathogenesis and treatment recommendations but comparable in diagnostic accuracy. However, no artificial intelligence system can replace clinical evaluation by a physician.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Based Clinical Decision Support in Pregnancy Specific Dermatological Lesions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for de novo small-molecule design, but the practical and translational utility of generated candidates depends on the configuration of the entire discovery workflow rather than on generative model architecture alone. This review adopts a workflow-based perspective on generative molecular design, tracing the process from existing molecular data sets, preprocessing and representation, to molecule generation, conditioning, candidate prioritization, evaluation, and iterative refinement. It examines how generative AI model families, constraints, and predictive oracles interact within this pipeline, and evaluates generated candidates using intrinsic metrics, computational assessments, and experimental and translational evidence. Active learning, computational and experimental feedback, and human expert input are further discussed as mechanisms for closed-loop refinement. Across these stages, we identify data construction and representation choices, oracle quality, evaluation protocols, and the availability of informative feedback as major determinants of how model performance should be interpreted and whether generated structures progress toward biologically and translationally meaningful candidates, with selected examples. In conclusion, reliable generative drug discovery requires coordinated design across the entire workflow rather than isolated advances in individual components.

Abstract Background To evaluate the clinical performance of a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiographic imaging compared with its predecessor across multiple imaging modes, anatomic regions, and endovascular specialties. Materials and methods This retrospective, comparative, randomized, paired, and blinded multicenter reader study included anonymized images acquired during clinically indicated endovascular interventions at 11 institutions in the United States and Europe. A total of 553 image series from 182 patients representing 51 procedure types across interventional radiology, neurointervention, cardiology, and pediatric cardiology were processed using both the AI-based and predecessor image processing algorithms. Thirteen board-certified physicians independently evaluated paired images using five-point Likert scales for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details. The primary endpoint was non-inferiority of overall image quality. Secondary endpoints evaluated superiority across image quality metrics using a predefined hierarchical testing strategy. Results The AI-based image processing algorithm demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality in 98.9% of all evaluations (95% confidence interval [CI], 98%–100%), meeting the primary endpoint across all imaging modes, anatomic regions, and predefined subgroups. Superiority of the AI-based algorithm was demonstrated for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details across fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. Overall image quality superiority was not demonstrated for digital subtraction angiography, likely reflecting the intrinsically higher signal-to-noise characteristics of these acquisitions.
evidence_items.title: Clinical evaluation of a novel artificial intelligence-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiography

evidence_items.summary: Study on survey of post harvest pathogen, field and storage pests and diseases of three varieties of sugarcane found in Port Harcourt was carried out in the Department of Plant Science and Biotechnology and Rivers State Teaching and Research Farm, all in the Rivers State University. Three sugar cane varieties identified based on stem colour viz: Kasha Cane-B51415 (Dark green), Anancy-BJ6183 (Green) and Kava Rangi-B64.277 (Red stem) were collected from Port Harcourt. The cultural laboratory technique was used for the microbial study while the hand book of South African Sugarcane Research Institute was used for field pests and diseases identification. Microbial shelf-life evaluation further revealed the red variety to contain reduced bacterial (3.8 x106 , 3.5 x106 and 2.2x106 cfu/g) and fungal (0.7 x104 , 1.3 x104 and 1.3 x104 cfu/g) loads for months 1, 2 and 3 respectively than other varieties within the storage months. A total of three bacterial organisms (Bacillus sp, Pseudomonas sp, Staphylococcus sp) and three fungal organisms (Aspergillus niger, A. flavus, Yeast) were isolated within the months of storage. Four field pests were observed viz: locust, aphid, trash caterpillar and fall army worm. However, none was recorded on the red variety. Five field diseases were observed including streak, red rot, rust, leaf spot and smut. The green variety recorded lowest number of prevailing field diseases. Generally, the three varieties of sugar cane performed differently with respect to pest and diseases.
evidence_items.title: Microbial Contamination, Field Diseases and Pests of Three Sugarcane Varieties Found in Port Harcourt

evidence_items.summary: Nuclear segmentation across patient-derived organoids (PDOs) is complicated by differences in morphology, staining, image scale, and acquisition format. We present ARIPA, an automated human-in-the-loop (HITL) system that coordinates pre-trained segmentation tools through a vision-language model (VLM)-based agentic planning, verification, and refinement loop for hematoxylin and eosin images of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded PDOs. In contrast to existing tools, ARIPA does not require training and achieves good performance. Tissue-aware tiling and image-derived calibration initialize segmentation; optional expert corrections guide configuration search and light-weight object-level rules without retraining or fine-tuning the pre-trained segmentation networks. We evaluated initial ARIPA predictions on more than 50,000 nuclei from 19 images of breast, head and neck, and lung patient-derived cancer PDOs, where nuclear segmentation was challenging due to its 3D structure and variation in imaging layers and malignant cell morphology. Performance was evaluated on agent-selected models before expert feedback, after feedback from the initial runs excluding direct expert edits, and in comparison to a custom-trained HoVer-Net model previously published by our group. At a minimum polygon intersection over union (IoU) of 0.5, image-macro F1 was 0.8380 before feedback, 0.9849 after feedback, and 0.4713 for HoVer-Net. Mean area under the F1 score versus IoU curve was 0.8013, 0.9700, and 0.4317, respectively. The mean paired F1 increase after feedback was 0.1468, with increases in 17 out of the total 19 images and no changes in the remaining two. Ground truth nuclei annotations were created by expert review and editing of ARIPA's post-feedback outputs. In this cohort, ARIPA outperformed the custom-trained HoVer-Net, and its performance was improved further following expert-guided HITL refinement.
evidence_items.title: ARIPA: Agentic Reasoning for Image-based Pathology Analysis

evidence_items.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems evolve toward increasingly autonomous and agentic capabilities, responsibility for decisions becomes distributed across autonomous agents, human stakeholders, and organizations, creating significant accountability challenges. While Agentic AI research has largely focused on technical mechanisms such as alignment, monitoring, explainability, and safety, comparatively little empirical evidence explains how Organizational Accountability is maintained in practice. This study investigates whether Organizational Accountability is explained primarily by technical autonomy, Individual Accountability Avoidance, or organizational governance capabilities. Drawing on a multinational survey of AI practitioners from the United States, Germany, China, and South Africa, the study examines AI projects spanning different levels of automation as a practical proxy for the transition toward Agentic AI. Factor analysis identified the underlying accountability constructs, while correlation and hierarchical regression analyses evaluated the relationships among Automation Level, Moral Disengagement, Responsibility Redirection, Structural Accountability Reinforcement, and Organizational Accountability. The findings indicate that Organizational Accountability is only weakly associated with increasing technical autonomy and is not consistently explained by Individual Accountability Avoidance. Instead, Structural Accountability Reinforcement exhibited the strongest and most consistent relationships with Organizational Accountability, particularly Transparent Compliance and Responsible AI Governance. Additional moderation analyses found no evidence that governance capabilities mitigated the effects of Moral Disengagement or Responsibility Redirection, indicating that governance contributes directly to Organizational Accountability rather than offsetting accountability avoidance behaviors.
evidence_items.title: Organizational Accountability in Agentic AI: A Governance Capability Perspective

evidence_items.summary: Accurate protein complex structure modeling requires knowledge of complex stoichiometry, yet the copy numbers of individual subunits are often unknown. Consequently, predicting protein complex stoichiometry has emerged as a major challenge in recent years. Here, we present StoiAgent, a large language model (LLM)-powered AI agent that automates the retrieval and integration of sequence, structural, and literature evidence to predict stoichiometry while preserving interpretable reasoning traces (chain of thoughts) of its evidence assessment and ranking decision. An open-weight LLM model, Qwen3.6-27B, is used by StoiAgent as the LLM backbone to combine sequences, structural templates, AlphaFold3 structure predictions, and literature evidence, and perform stoichiometry candidate generation and ranking. On 56 CASP17 protein complex targets, it achieves top-1 accuracy of 75.0%, which represents a 23.2 percentage-point improvement over PreStoi with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%) and matches the top-1 accuracy of StoPred. Moreover, StoiAgent has a higher top-3 and top-5 accuracy than StoPred (85.7% versus 80.4% and 87.5% versus 85.7%, respectively). Furthermore, it outperforms general-purpose frontier LLMs, including ChatGPT and Gemini, in stoichiometry prediction. Case studies further illustrate how StoiAgent evaluates competing assembly hypotheses by integrating complementary evidence, with recorded reasoning traces documenting its decision-making process. Overall, StoiAgent demonstrates the potential of LLM-powered AI agents to improve protein complex stoichiometry prediction through the automated integration of diverse sources of evidence while providing interpretable explanations to guide downstream structure modeling.
evidence_items.title: Accurate and interpretable protein complex stoichiometry prediction through agentic AI with StoiAgent

evidence_items.summary: Scientific figure quality is bound to the manuscript: a crop can be visually clear and still contradict its caption or the paragraph that cites it. Most image quality assessment and chart-understanding methods target a detached visual surface or a question-answering score, rather than alignment among the figure, its caption, and the citing text. A single end-to-end prompt that sees the image and the text together still mixes what is visible with what the caption and the citing paragraph claim, so fluent wording can raise a visual score and missing text can be treated as low quality. To address this gap, we introduce SciFigQual-Bench, a manuscript-linked benchmark for published CS-conference figures that binds each figure to its caption and to index-resolved citing paragraphs, and scores visual clarity, layout, caption consistency, context consistency, and misleading risk, leaving a dimension unevaluated when its evidence is absent. SFQ-Agent reads the image and the text in separate calls and records modality-specific evidence. A cross-modal judge scores caption and citing-text alignment from those reports, and a deterministic runner keeps the visual scores, sets misleading risk by a fixed rule, and applies the written caps, so each dimension follows the rubric instead of a single end-to-end prompt. Experiments comparing this staged judge with single-pass and OCR-sidecar protocols find the closest point-estimate fit to mean human ratings under staged judging, while the gap between protocols remains small. Caption consistency remains the main gap, and agreement with the rater mean answers a different question from agreement among human raters. Project page: https://frankdengai.github.io/SciFigQual-Bench/
evidence_items.title: SciFigQual-Bench: Scientific Figure Quality Assessment with Manuscript-Linked Context

evidence_items.summary: Localizing targets in $360^\circ$ environments requires combining global context with fine-grained evidence despite projection distortion and horizontal wrap-around. Uneven directional coverage compounds these challenges, particularly for seam-adjacent and polar targets. We present SPIRAL-360, a geometry-aware framework with separately trained single-turn and multi-turn models for panoramic localization. Spherically Stratified Replay (SSR) broadens directional coverage through stratified sampling and consistent transformations of panoramas, target annotations, and tool trajectories. TapSphere incorporates spherical distance priors into panoramic visual attention, while Spherical Direction Regularization (SDR) complements coordinate-token prediction with auxiliary direction supervision during training. The single-turn model predicts directly from the panorama, while the multi-turn model inspects tool-generated perspective views. We construct SPIRAL-360 Search, a curated dataset of trajectories interleaving reasoning, projection actions, and visual observations. Both models undergo full-parameter supervised fine-tuning followed by policy optimization. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art localization on S360 and competitive cross-dataset transfer, including H$^*$Bench. Systematic ablations support the effectiveness of this geometric learning design.
evidence_items.title: SPIRAL-360: Stratified Panoramic Instruction Replay and Angular Learning for Visual Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Unlike humans, who learn new concepts from a continuous visual stream, existing personalized vision-language models (VLMs) internalize a predefined concept set during training and operate on static images or offline videos. They cannot register a concept that a user defines in the middle of a stream, nor recall the earlier moments in which it appeared. We formalize this task as Personalized Streaming Video Understanding (PSVU) and introduce PSVU-Bench, the first benchmark for this task, which annotates 132 videos with timestamped questions. Its Concept-Definition, Real-Time and Past-Time QA ask a model to register concepts at arbitrary timestamps, recognize their current state, including user-defined actions, and retrieve their historical evidence. We propose PEARL, a strong plug-and-play baseline that stores user-defined concepts apart from archived video clips and rewrites each query with concept descriptions to retrieve the relevant history. Grounding a named concept in video is a skill shared by all concepts. We therefore construct PSVU-10K, a training set of verified concept questions on public internet videos, and train the retriever and answering VLM of PEARL on it once. Concepts defined at test time still require no training. Applied to three architectures without training, PEARL improves Real-Time QA by 15.05% and Past-Time QA by 12.60% on average over the corresponding offline models, and all three surpass existing online video models on both QA types. Training further improves PEARL on Qwen3-VL-8B by 8.66% on Real-Time QA and 9.39% on Past-Time QA, with gains in every category. Code, data and models are available at https://github.com/Yuanhong-Zheng/PEARL.
evidence_items.title: PEARL: Personalized Streaming Video Understanding with Runtime-Defined Concepts

evidence_items.summary: We evaluated Jev, a non-generative decision model, for title and abstract screening using 4527 records from two systematic reviews of bipolar disorder treatments previously used in our 2024 Journal of Medical Internet Research study. Human decisions to retain records for full-text assessment served as the reference. In the primary analysis, Jev answered yes-or-no questions (Noul); at a prespecified 50% cutoff, sensitivity and specificity were 99.6% and 98.9% for light therapy and 93.2% and 93.5% for adjunctive pharmacotherapy. For direct model comparison, Jev used explicit include/exclude options (Choice) and the same prompts as GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra. Jev Choice achieved sensitivity and specificity similar to or higher than those of GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra, while API charges per 1000 records were US$0.043 for Jev, US$0.57 for GPT-5 mini, and US$7.39 for GPT-6 Astra. Jev retained all reports ultimately included in both reviews across all tested conditions and runs. Although these findings do not establish that decision models can replace human reviewers, they support Jev as a promising, low-cost alternative to the tested generative LLM configurations for assisting human title and abstract screening. Independent validation across diverse review topics is needed to assess Jev’s generalizability and utility in human-supervised screening workflows.
evidence_items.title: Title and Abstract Screening for Systematic Reviews with Jev, a Decision Model: Comparison with Generative Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Importance Hospital discharge summaries are essential for continuity of care, but fragmented electronic health record (EHR) data can compromise their quality and safety. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for clinical documentation tasks despite limited evidence regarding their performance in health care settings compared with the current standard of care. Objective To evaluate clinician acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries derived from EHRs compared with routine clinician-written summaries. Design, Setting, and Participants In this retrospective comparative effectiveness study using a prespecified noninferiority framework, acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries was compared with clinician-authored discharge summaries. Admission records from 5 London hospitals for September 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, were evaluated against the full admission record by practicing physicians. Admissions were eligible only if the clinician-authored discharge summary contained identifiable clinical summary, plan and requested actions, and information given sections. Data analysis was conducted from July 2025 to February 2026. Intervention LLM-generated summaries were produced using GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI) and a clinician-codesigned prompt. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was clinician signoff with no or minor edits, derived from 2 sequential questions: (1) whether the reviewer would sign the summary and (2) whether no, minor, or major edits were required. A 5–percentage-point noninferiority margin was prespecified. Secondary outcomes assessed accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, poor; 2, fair; 3, good; 4, very good; and 5, excellent) and potential harmfulness of missing or incorrect information (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, no harm; 2, minor harm; 3, moderate harm; 4, high harm; and 5, extremely high harm).
evidence_items.title: Clinician Acceptance of Large Language Model–Generated Discharge Summaries

evidence_items.summary: Software issue resolution task aims to address real-world issues in software repositories based on natural language descriptions provided by users, representing a key aspect of software maintenance. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs) in reasoning and generative capabilities, LLM-based approaches have made significant progress in automated software issue resolution. However, real-world software issue resolution is inherently complex and requires long-horizon reasoning, iterative exploration, and feedback-driven decision-making that demand agentic capabilities beyond conventional single-step approaches. Recently, LLM-based agentic systems have become a promising research direction for software issue resolution, since the related literature has experienced explosive growth. Advancements in agentic software issue resolution not only greatly enhance software maintenance efficiency and quality but also provide a realistic environment for validating agentic systems’ reasoning, planning, and execution capabilities, bridging AI and software engineering. This work presents a systematic survey of 242 recent studies at the forefront of LLM-based agentic software issue resolution research. It outlines the general workflow of the task and establishes a taxonomy across three dimensions: benchmarks, techniques, and empirical studies. Furthermore, it highlights how reinforcement learning has become an increasingly important training paradigm for agentic systems in software engineering. Finally, it summarizes key challenges and outlines promising directions for future research. The artifacts’ page accompanying this survey is at https://github.com/ZhonghaoJiang/Awesome-Issue-Solving.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Software Issue Resolution with Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.
evidence_items.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games

rationale: Matched: benchmark, synthetic data, test set
evidence_items.summary: Vision-based navigation systems for orbit must be trained almost entirely on synthetic imagery, because real labelled images of a given spacecraft in flight rarely exist. Benchmarks like SPEED+ are built for that situation: the training set comes from a simulator, and the test sets are real images of a satellite mockup under two kinds of lighting. That simulator approximates how light reflects off mylar and aluminium, and like every scientific simulator it is misspecified. Its error is radiometric, since it misses the specular highlights, hard shadows and sensor saturation common in real images. We probe the resulting synthetic-to-real gap, the central risk for such systems, with a deliberately simple monocular pose estimator. In a 2x2 study of backbone adaptation and photometric augmentation, trained on synthetic images and tested on both real hardware-in-the-loop domains, we find three things. (1) The model does not know it is failing: regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox, so a wrong pose carries the confidence of a correct one. (2) Transfer is asymmetric: scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moved the harshly lit sunlamp domain by only 0.05 rad, under twice its seed s.d., whereas adapting the backbone's last stage carried 63-83% of its extra synthetic gain to both real domains. (3) Once the backbone adapts, augmentation helps only in the direction it models: our photometric stack improved the diffusely lit lightbox domain from 1.17 to 0.99 rad on every seed but moved sunlamp no more than seed-to-seed variation, while with the backbone frozen it helped sunlamp more. Every post-review experiment was pre-registered, and the code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record are at https://github.com/lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation.
evidence_items.title: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.
evidence_items.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements

evidence_items.summary: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
evidence_items.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents

evidence_items.summary: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.
evidence_items.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
evidence_items.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?

evidence_items.summary: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.
evidence_items.title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration

evidence_items.summary: π^4 is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, π^4 achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.
evidence_items.title: π^4: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion

evidence_items.summary: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.
evidence_items.title: ALIVE: Making Streaming Video Models Interactive

evidence_items.summary: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.
evidence_items.title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning

evidence_items.summary: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% to 82.7% and 14.3% to 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% to 90.5% and 21.9% to 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec. Website: https://auxspec.org
evidence_items.title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions

evidence_items.summary: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.
evidence_items.title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.
evidence_items.title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.
evidence_items.title: MInfoVisQA: A Multilingual Benchmark for Information-Rich Visual Question Answering

Preserve the nuisance response before applying subtraction; otherwise the receiving laboratory cannot reconstruct what was removed. What the diamond can and cannot see NV resonance shifts can respond to axial field, temperature and other perturbations. A point on a fluorescent image does not, by itself, identify a nerve current. A paired spectral witness, independent temperature logging and a known source-return geometry must establish field sensitivity before any biological proposal. Near-sensor experimental evidence is not a proof of clinically useful access to deep peripheral nerves. The geometry gap becomes a new question rather than a hidden extrapolation. Volition as a task construct Intention is studied through instructed choices, consented reports and behavior. The experiment cannot read an unexpressed private mental state merely because a classifier performs well. Separate cue, preparation, execution and rest; use matched eye, muscle and breathing references and participant-held-out tests. Qigong and Xianggong may inspire questions of attention and movement. Their language is not a physical calibration standard and does not define a magnetic carrier. Classical does not mean weak SQUID magnetometers are quantum devices too. A serious benchmark distinguishes sensing elements and full systems explicitly; an appropriately chosen fluxgate or induction coil may be relevant in its own band. Compare source waveform, standoff, shielding, bandwidth, acquisition time and full system energy. Define the valid comparison before observing the result. A limited comparison may support a practical engineering tradeoff, not a universal victory of a technology category. Noise can carry structure Shared environmental fields, feedback currents and trigger-correlated motion can survive averaging. A square-root improvement assumes independence or a justified covariance law. Repeat blank measurements and concealed injections under realistic correlated and heavy-tailed disturbances; record exclusions and their effect on uncertainty. The noise model is a research object. A poor fit should narrow the claim rather than motivate post hoc removal of the troublesome data. The formula atlas is a contract The thirty equations are candidate physical or statistical relations, not fitted measurements. Their units and assumptions establish what a future test can mean. Each relation is paired with a synthetic surface and an explicit competing explanation. The plotted parameter ranges illustrate sensitivity and ambiguity, not recommended exposure settings. The atlas may be revised where the device model fails; retaining failed assumptions is part of the scientific record. Forty-two three-dimensional questions The model atlas varies two coordinates at a time to reveal a slope, degeneracy, threshold, tradeoff or uncertainty envelope. All arrays are deterministic examples. CSV data, a model manifest and a regeneration program permit an independent reconstruction. None contains actual participant measurements. Use the surfaces to plan discriminant measurements. A visually persuasive surface cannot replace a calibrated witness.
