evidence_items.summary: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.
evidence_items.title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence has been booming in the field of natural language processing, but the existing intelligent algorithms for grammatical correction of English writing mostly focus on single text modal information, making it difficult to mine multi-dimensional features, and the accuracy is poor when dealing with complex errors and subtle deviations. Therefore, a method for grammatical correction of English writing based on a multimodal large language model is proposed. The subword granularity segmentation method and NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) segmenter are used to preprocess the text, and a semantic encoder based on BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) and Bi-GRU (Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit) is constructed to obtain semantic information. Gating units are added to each modal feature to achieve fusion. In the decoding stage, a hybrid attention mechanism is used to balance the probability by borrowing the replication mechanism, and beam search is combined with a length factor optimization strategy to complete the correction. Experiments show that the overall average F0.5(F-measure with β=0.5) score reaches 0.512, which is 21.1% higher than the comparison method. In terms of GLEU (General Language Evaluation Understanding (metric)) score, the data scale is 12.7% ahead when it is small, and it is 14.2% ahead when it is increased, and the performance fluctuation is only 1/3 of the comparison method. Experiments show that this method significantly improves the accuracy of error correction and provides a reliable and efficient solution for this field.
evidence_items.title: A Grammatical Correction Method for English Writing Based on a Multimodal Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs), have enabled intelligent perception, reasoning, and decision-making in complex human–computer interaction scenarios, providing new technical foundations for optimizing online language instruction. However, existing online English teaching strategies remain largely experience-driven and lack adaptive optimization mechanisms supported by computational models. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an AI-empowered teaching strategy optimization framework for online English classrooms based on large language models. The framework integrates natural language processing for instructional content understanding, knowledge graph modeling for structured pedagogical knowledge representation, and behavioral perception algorithms for real-time analysis of learner interactions. By jointly modeling instructional context, learner states, and classroom behaviors, the proposed system enables dynamic generation and adaptive adjustment of teaching strategies. A prototype system was implemented and evaluated through controlled comparative experiments conducted in real online classroom environments. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly improves learning outcomes, classroom engagement, and instructional feedback efficiency compared with conventional online teaching strategies. Beyond online English instruction, the proposed framework exhibits strong interdisciplinary applicability and can be extended to other domains involving adaptive human-centered decision-making, such as intelligent tutoring systems, digital training platforms, and human–machine collaborative learning environments. The findings confirm the effectiveness of large language models in supporting intelligent teaching strategy optimization and provide a practical computational solution for enhancing the quality and adaptability of online instructional systems.
evidence_items.title: An AI-Empowered Large Language Model Framework for Computational Optimization of Online English Teaching Strategies

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background AI is increasingly impacting health care. Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have shown potential in supporting clinical decision-making. However, their application in dermatology, particularly in allergen avoidance counseling for contact dermatitis, remains underexplored. Objective This study aimed to demonstrate a potential use case for LLM responses in recommending allergen-free products for the management of contact allergies. Methods A total of 30 allergen groups included in the international standard patch test were assessed. ChatGPT (GPT-4) was used in this study from September 2023 to January 2024. For each allergen, ChatGPT was tasked with recommending 5 allergen-free products using 3 question formats of varying complexity. Responses were included if they specified a product and were manually classified by dermatologists into 5 categories: valid, invalid, cross-reaction, unknown, and unresponsive. Results ChatGPT provided 79.20% (1782/2250) valid responses, with 1.78% (40/2250) classified as invalid, 2% (45/2550) classified as cross-reactions, 8.67% (195/2250) classified as unknown, and 8.36% (188/2250) classified as unresponsive. The simplest question format yielded the highest proportion of valid recommendations (640/750, 85.33%). ChatGPT performed best when recommending cosmetics (1233/1365, 90.33%) and medications (198/240, 82.5%). However, lower validity rates were observed for recommendations involving certain sensitive allergens, including fragrance mixes and para-phenylenediamine (PPD), with frequent cross-reactive recommendations related to Peru balsam. Conclusions The version of ChatGPT evaluated in this study showed potential as a supplementary tool for allergen avoidance counseling. However, its recommendations require verification and should not replace clinician guidance or established allergen avoidance resources.
evidence_items.title: Using a Large Language Model Chatbot for Allergen Avoidance Counseling in Contact Dermatitis: Quantitative Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Narratives are a universal part of natural human experience. As experimental stimuli, narratives allow scientists to study complex mental processes with direct relevance to everyday experience. These analyses typically require manual labeling of key event features. Such characterization of narrative stimuli are extremely labor-intensive and prone to subjectivity. Automated tools could reduce these difficulties and enable scaling to longer, varied stimuli by exposing the exact quantities computed. We address this by introducing a metric that uses open-weight LLMs to compute contextual information gain. Our metric correlates with human ratings of event importance and causal centrality, critically distinguishing the latter from semantic centrality, thus overcoming limitations of existing automated tools. The metric similarly captures shared coactivation in the default mode network, a network implicated in narrative comprehension. Taken together, these results validate an automated, empirically-grounded tool that researchers can use to identify behaviorally- and neurally-relevant computational quantities in naturalistic stimuli.
evidence_items.title: Scaling up naturalistic narrative research: A reproducible large language model-based tool for evaluating contextual information gain

evidence_items.summary: Mobile manipulators can move between storage locations and handle goods, but transferring the semantic capabilities of foundation models to dependable warehouse operations remains constrained by execution interfaces, data coverage, and operating conditions. This thematic critical review examines perception, reasoning, planning and execution, and data and generalization. It compares hierarchical approaches with vision-language-action models and assesses their relevance to warehouse tasks using representative studies. Its distinctive value lies in relating model interfaces and transfer limits to warehouse order fulfillment, where stock-keeping unit (SKU) verification, shelf access, and onboard resource limits must be considered together. The evidence indicates that foundation models reorganize selected interfaces between observations, task descriptions, and actions; they do not remove the need for geometric feasibility checks, low-level control, or failure recovery. Open-vocabulary recognition must be connected to item-level verification, while semantic generalization should be distinguished from the acquisition of new motor skills. Reported transfer gains also depend on the task, embodiment, and adaptation budget. The review identifies order completion, coordinated base-arm motion, and measurable adaptation costs as priorities for research and evaluation. These conclusions support method selection and experimental design rather than a claim of validated warehouse deployment.
evidence_items.title: Warehouse Mobile Manipulation with Large Language Models and Foundation Models

organizations: University of California Irvine Medical Center
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Medical students often struggle transitioning from preclinical coursework to clinical environments. Simulation-based training can bridge this gap but can be resource intensive. Large language models (LLMs) provide a scalable resource that can augment traditional training. However, their effects on learning outcomes and student perceptions are currently not understood. This study aims to evaluate medical student knowledge acquisition and perception of the utility of simplified LLM-based clinical simulation. Methods Using the RISE framework, a structured simulation was designed to assess medical student knowledge of acute asthma exacerbation management. ZotGPT, an institutional GPT-4 based platform was utilized. Medical students completed pre- and post-simulation assessments assessing knowledge, confidence, and perceptions of simulation utility. Subgroup analysis was stratified by time spent completing the simulation. Statistical analyses included Wilcoxon signal-rank and McNemar tests. Results A total of 155 students participated. The simulation significantly improved perceived understanding of key treatment steps, including initial bronchodilator and steroid therapy (p = 0.001), magnesium sulfate escalation (p = 0.002), refractory management (p = 0.021), and discharge planning (p = 0.005). Students rated the simulation as more useful than non-simulation learning tools (p = 0.017) and noninferior to in-person simulation (p = 0.226). Confidence in asthma management increased (p < 0.001), but objective knowledge gains were not observed, with balanced correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct responses for intermediate steps. Longer engagement (> 600 seconds) was associated with greater perceived benefit. Simulations were deemed helpful for learning (94.7%), and most students preferred immediate feedback (68.4%).
evidence_items.title: Assessing the Learning Gains and User Experience of Large Language Model Simulations for Clinical Medical Education: A Pilot Observational Study

organizations: Sichuan Academy of Environmental Policy and Planning
evidence_items.summary: Abstract As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to gather, process and disseminate scientific information, concerns have grown about their identity-related biases. However, national-background biases in scientific evaluation remain insufficiently understood. Existing studies are limited to a narrow range of countries, abbreviated materials and/or simplified evaluation criteria, and have reported inconsistent findings. Moreover, differences in the textual evaluations generated by LLMs have seldom been quantified. Here, we used four popular LLMs to evaluate 292 full-text manuscripts from 28 journals across 8 research fields under 12 assigned national backgrounds, yielding 14,016 manuscript assessments, each covering 28 evaluative dimensions. Further comment-based rescoring tests were conducted to quantify differences in their textual evaluations. The results showed systematic differences in both scores and comments despite unchanged scientific content, with the magnitude and statistical significance these differences varying across national backgrounds. Under different national backgrounds, LLMs could offer different views on the same issue, and give different scores alongside similar textual evaluation. Researchers and decision-makers should be aware of these biases associated with source identity, including national background, when using LLMs for information gathering and processing.
evidence_items.title: National-background bias in scientific evaluation based on large language models
Benchmark for self-organized criticality

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being considered as tools for computational social science, yet their implications for survey and public-opinion research remain insufficiently understood. This study examines whether and how they can serve as methodological instruments for estimating aggregate public opinion under out-of-sample conditions. Across three studies, commercial and open-source LLMs are evaluated against recent Pew Research Centre surveys. Study 1 shows that GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can approximate national-level response distributions more accurately than uniform, normal-distribution, and historical-average baselines, with GPT-4 achieving mean absolute errors of approximately 4–8.5%. However, the models also exhibit important threats to validity, including underrepresentation of Republican viewpoints, underestimation of uncertainty, and, in some cases, overly homogeneous response distributions. Study 2 extends the analysis to GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama 3.3, showing that aggregate predictive accuracy generalises across models but that partisan alignment and distributional fidelity are model- and topic-dependent. Study 3 demonstrates that collective-level estimation is more valid than aggregating persona-based individual simulations, which produce substantially higher error and stronger homogeneity bias. Ablation tests further indicate that predictions are relatively robust to role prompts and temperature settings but sensitive to survey-item context. These findings suggest that LLMs may be useful as exploratory and supplementary tools in public-opinion research. However, the responsible use of LLMs requires explicit validation against human data, attention to bias and uncertainty, and careful integration with established principles of survey design.
evidence_items.title: Public opinion surveys with large language models: methodological opportunities and validity risks

organizations: Surgery, David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, Los Angeles, CA
evidence_items.summary: In December 2025, the Food and Drug Administration assessed and qualified the first artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool for use in drug development trials; this AI system evaluates digital liver biopsies for steatohepatitis and fibrosis. However, AI is still being investigated before it can be applied directly to patient care in the field of Hepatology. Current patient-facing applications at most institutions are limited to assistive tools such as computer-aided polyp detection and large language model documentation tools that draft clinic notes and patient communications, although there exist radiographic and pathologic liver AI tools that could function at and may even exceed human capabilities. This review provides a broad introduction to AI and highlights clinical research that use AI to enhance the diagnosis, prognostication, and management of liver diseases. It will also discuss the challenges that will need to be overcome before AI can be adopted to clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Hepatology

organizations: The University of Western Australia, School of Physics, Mathematics and Computing A , , , .
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and, more recently, generative AI (GenAI) models are becoming increasingly prevalent in the healthcare setting. For microbiology professionals, these technologies create opportunities to improve diagnostic workflows, analyse complex laboratory data, support education and professional development, summarise evidence, and assist with quality improvement. They also introduce risks, including automation bias, data leakage, poor generalisability, hallucinated or unverifiable outputs, privacy breaches, and unclear accountability. This article proposes a practical curriculum framework for microbiology professionals that treats GenAI as a distinct educational priority rather than a minor extension of conventional data, statistics or ML training. The curriculum framework is organised around six domains: (1) foundations of AI, ML and GenAI; (2) microbiology data and knowledge literacy; (3) critical appraisal, validation and evaluation; (4) responsible use of GenAI in microbiology practice and education; (5) implementation, governance, regulation and professional accountability; and (6) communication, collaboration and lifelong learning. The goal is not to train every microbiology professional as a data scientist. The aim is to develop AI-literate practitioners who can critically evaluate tools, use GenAI safely, participate in governance, communicate uncertainty, and ensure that AI-enabled practice remains grounded in microbiological expertise and patient safety.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy for microbiology professionals

organizations: Department of Hospital Therapeutic Dentistry, Tashkent State Medical University, Tashkent, Uzbekistan
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technological developments in modern healthcare, creating new opportunities for improving diagnosis, treatment, patient monitoring, clinical decisionmaking, and healthcare management. The increasing availability of electronic health records, medical imaging, genomic information, wearable devices, and other forms of digital health data has created an environment in which AI-based systems can identify complex patterns that may be difficult to recognize through conventional approaches. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and generative AI are currently being investigated and implemented across multiple medical specialties. In clinical practice, AI can support radiological image interpretation, early disease detection, risk prediction, personalized treatment selection, drug development, clinical documentation, and remote patient monitoring. These applications may contribute to earlier diagnosis, improved clinical efficiency, reduced workload, and more individualized patient care. AI-enabled medical devices have also increasingly entered clinical practice, particularly in radiology and cardiology. However, the successful integration of AI into healthcare requires careful attention to data quality, algorithmic bias, patient privacy, transparency, cybersecurity, clinical validation, and professional accountability. AI should therefore be regarded as a clinical support technology rather than a replacement for healthcare professionals. This review examines the major clinical applications and potential benefits of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare and discusses the principal challenges that must be addressed to ensure safe, ethical, effective, and patient-centered implementation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Modern Healthcare: Clinical Applications and Benefits

evidence_items.summary: Environmental contamination is increasingly recognised as a human rights issue engaging State obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). In Cannavacciuolo and Others v Italy , the European Court of Human Rights held that prolonged environmental exposure may trigger positive obligations under Article 2 ECHR, requiring public authorities to identify, monitor and mitigate foreseeable risks to life. Implementing these obligations depends on the integration of environmental, clinical and epidemiological evidence. This paper argues that legal medicine can provide the methodological bridge between legal principles and scientific assessment. We propose an Integrated Environmental Medico-Legal Assessment Framework (I-EMAF), a conceptual model supporting transparent, multidisciplinary and evidence-based evaluation of environmental contamination. Rather than introducing new investigative methods, I-EMAF organises established scientific approaches within a coherent medico-legal structure to assist courts, public authorities and healthcare systems to implement their Article 2 obligations.
evidence_items.title: Environmental contamination, human rights and medico-legal responsibility after Cannavacciuolo and Others v Italy (ECtHR)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) is widely used to identify genomic regions associated with a protein of interest, including transcription factors and other chromatin-associated proteins. However, the reliability of ChIP-seq experiments is questionable, because they often do not recover expected transcription factor-DNA binding sites. A robust workflow is essential for reliably detecting protein-associated genomic regions, particularly in plant tissues. Results Here we present a complete and robust plant ChIP-seq workflow from tissue harvest to annotated peaks, generating high signal-to-noise ratio, developed for approximately 2–3 g of 7-day-old Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings expressing a tagged protein of interest. The wet-lab procedure comprises formaldehyde crosslinking under vacuum infiltration, isolation of nuclei, detergent-assisted chromatin extraction, sonication, and affinity enrichment using RFP-Trap Magnetic Agarose beads. A particularly critical, yet often overlooked, parameter for achieving a reproducible high signal-to-noise ratio is the optimization of the balance between the amount of input chromatin containing the tagged protein and the volume of affinity beads used for immunoprecipitation. Then, affinity enrichment is followed by stringent sequential washing, reversal of crosslinks and column-based purification of ChIP DNA, with input chromatin and mock IP samples processed in parallel as controls. Purified DNA is converted into dual-indexed Illumina libraries using the TruSeq DNA Nano kit, quantified by qPCR and sequenced in paired-end mode (2×151 bp) on an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus. Reads are then quality-trimmed with fastp, aligned to the TAIR10 reference genome with Bowtie2, and peaks are called against matched input controls with MACS3 and annotated with ChIPseeker (https://github.com/mhajheidari/FLC-ChIP-seq-analysis).
evidence_items.title: FLC genomic occupancy as a biological benchmark for plant ChIP-seq: a complete workflow from crosslinking to motif validation

evidence_items.summary: As artificial intelligence systems evolve beyond conversational interfaces into multi-step workflows capable of retrieving information, maintaining state, invoking tools, delegating tasks, and acting across external systems, electronic discovery faces increasingly complex evidentiary questions. A user-facing transcript or current system configuration may not establish what information an AI system received, what instructions and controls governed its behavior, what actions it was authorized to perform, or what consequences resulted from a disputed historical execution.This white paper examines the application of United States federal civil discovery and evidence law to AI and agentic systems. Drawing on emerging judicial decisions and established electronic discovery principles, it analyzes relevance, proportionality, preservation, possession, custody or control, privilege, production, authentication, and expert proof. It identifies potential evidentiary sources across system and developer instructions, model configurations, retrieval-augmented generation, tool and API schemas, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, agent memory, orchestration, delegated authority, execution traces, configuration histories, and downstream business records.The paper advances reconstructable execution state as a proposition-centered analytical framework for identifying the minimum historically accurate evidence necessary to evaluate a disputed AI execution. It distinguishes technical capability from authorization, attempted actions from completed effects, present-day configurations from historical conditions, and contemporaneous records from inference or later reconstruction.Integrating recent AI-related discovery developments with practical preservation, collection, and evidentiary methods, the paper proposes an execution-centered approach to identifying relevant sources, reconstructing historical system behavior, and evaluating evidentiary reliability.
evidence_items.title: Discovering Agentic AI: Discovery, Preservation, and Proof in AI and Agentic Systems

evidence_items.summary: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.
evidence_items.title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules

evidence_items.summary: Generative novel view synthesis (NVS) employs a diffusion model to render a static or dynamic scene from a target camera view. Explicit warp methods complete a reprojection of the source with video diffusion models, and implicit methods encode the camera parameters or 3D cues. Both add inference overhead, and the generated layout often drifts from the ground truth. We present WaveView, which injects the warped source into the phase of the initial noise of a pretrained generator. The Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform (DT-CWPT) allows local and anisotropic phase injection. The generator is thus constrained less in disoccluded regions and along the epipolar line. WaveView keeps the architecture and adds negligible overhead. On the DL3DV benchmark, it outperforms all baselines in every overlap bin. In the hardest bin, it gains 0.84 dB PSNR on the covisible region over MetaView, which shares its generator, while running 2.1 times faster. For dynamic NVS, fine-tuning AnyView with the same noise raises its zero-shot PSNR on AnyViewBench from 11.58 to 12.35 dB.
evidence_items.title: WaveView: The Novel View Is in the Noise

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.
evidence_items.title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow

evidence_items.summary: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.
evidence_items.title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning

evidence_items.summary: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy's own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce HINT-WAM, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in https://tuandattt.github.io/hintwam/.
evidence_items.title: HINT-WAM: Hindsight-Informed Training for World Action Models

evidence_items.summary: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. We formalize these metrics in a unified integral form and show that the weight of a local error decays as the (k+q)-th power of its size, where k is the dimension of the integration domain and q is determined by the penalty function. Guided by this analysis, we propose DrawScore, which projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines, as in engineering drawings, and applies a saturating penalty along the projected curves, so that the weight of a local error decays only linearly. Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders, and on outputs of existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs that IoU rates as nearly perfect. DrawScore further improves generation as a reinforcement learning reward and, for CAD generation from engineering drawings, serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth or an additional reward model. Our code is available at https://github.com/UESTC-Simon/DrawScore.
evidence_items.title: DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.
evidence_items.title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour

evidence_items.summary: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.
evidence_items.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration

evidence_items.summary: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.
evidence_items.title: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: The goal of this paper is to reduce the input token cost of Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) at inference time. Omni-LLMs reason jointly over audio, video and text, but the cost of the three streams is highly unbalanced: visual tokens account for the vast majority of the input, and are highly redundant. In this paper, we propose ReMo, a training-free framework that compresses visual tokens by redistributing their information across modalities: a visual token is kept only if its information appears nowhere else. ReMo achieves this in two ways: (i) it aligns audio and video in a shared space via closed-form calibration, and removes visual tokens already explained by the audio or by other visual tokens; and (ii) it replaces object-level visual tokens, identified by a lightweight object detector, with compact text proxies, short descriptions of each object and its location, conveying the same content in far fewer tokens. On Qwen2.5-Omni at two model scales, ReMo removes 54% of the input tokens with comparable accuracy. It performs comparably to the full-token model, reaching 101.2% and 101.4% of its average accuracy over five audio-visual benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Out of Sight, Still in Mind: Token Compression for Omni-LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.
evidence_items.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents

evidence_items.summary: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by a model, while a single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that a bias obscured in one feature space may be clearer in another. In this work, we propose CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing), a multi-view framework that allows samples to "sing in chorus" across diverse representation spaces to achieve robust cross-view consensus. CHORD aggregates aggregates within-class partitions in each view, which is a proxy for specifying candidate biases, to debias the target representation and classifier without bias supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks across vision, language, speech, and medical imaging show consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/davelee-uestc/chord_debiasing_public .
evidence_items.title: Let Samples Sing in Chorus: Mitigating Spurious Correlations via Cross-view Consensus

evidence_items.summary: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon
evidence_items.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference

evidence_items.summary: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill
evidence_items.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback

evidence_items.summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into N parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts Nin{4,8,16}. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.
evidence_items.title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates

evidence_items.summary: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
evidence_items.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers

evidence_items.summary: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.
evidence_items.title: VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context

evidence_items.summary: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce MedJev, a system one vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, MedJev removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, MedJev-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of 7.93\% and a 6.04times end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that MedJev-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.
evidence_items.title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding

evidence_items.summary: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.
evidence_items.title: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)

evidence_items.summary: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over π_{0.5}) at 92.7 ms latency.
evidence_items.title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models

evidence_items.summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly becoming a dominant paradigm for AI applications. Recently, there is a growing demand to deploy large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models locally on consumer PCs to balance data privacy, API costs, and inference efficiency. However, unlike datacenter servers with abundant DRAM, consumer devices are tightly constrained in both GPU VRAM and host RAM, forcing massive MoE weights to spill across VRAM, host RAM, and SSD. Under such spilling, we observe that existing systems fail to fully utilize this memory hierarchy, treating the tiers as independent caches and thrashing in inference.
  We present TIDEWAY, a system for efficient inference of large MoE models on memory-constrained consumer devices. Our core insight is to manage host RAM and GPU VRAM as a unified memory pool. Within this pool, TIDEWAY couples phase-aware memory layouts, which adapt to the distinct access patterns of prefill and decode, with an execution engine that optimizes CUDA Graph execution under expert paging. Our evaluations on representative consumer hardware with frontier MoE models demonstrate that TIDEWAY significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems. On average, TIDEWAY achieves speedups of 1.97x in end-to-end latency and 2.40x in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), along with 1.61x higher decode throughput against the fastest baseline.
  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/Tideway .
evidence_items.title: Tideway: Phase-Aware Tiered Memory Management for MoE Inference on Consumer Devices

evidence_items.summary: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.
evidence_items.title: PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling

evidence_items.summary: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.
evidence_items.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data

evidence_items.summary: Large language models have reduced the effort to generate code for interactive software with graphical user interfaces (GUIs). For such software, a key testing bottleneck is reaching a deep state, one that requires a long interaction history. The cost of reaching it recurs across commits, and the GUI automation that could amortize it assumes a DOM or accessibility tree that self-rendered engines do not expose. We introduce StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes a checkpoint, an artifact that restores that state and can be versioned and replayed, from a natural-language functional test case and read-only access to the target's source code. The checkpoint is restored through a per-application hook that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes once without hand-written hook code. Because a checkpoint can satisfy state checks while rendering incorrectly, checkpoints are scored by hybrid programmatic-state and visual evaluation: acceptance requires both a programmatic-state oracle and a visual oracle to pass. We calibrate the visual oracle against a blinded cross-VLM reference. We release DeepStateBench, 61 deep-state tasks across 10 interactive applications that span five language families and six rendering stacks, with source sizes from 874 to 7.2M lines. Across three registered models, a GUI agent seeded with synthesized checkpoints completes 10.4% of trials, compared with 0% without seeding under the same pixel action space, while StatePortal, which also delivers the target action through the hook, completes 27.5%. Over 1,361 replays of 112 checkpoints, 98.90% reproduce the original verdict with zero model calls, and the hybrid oracle detects 96.25% (77/80) of controlled visual faults invisible to programmatic-state checks alone. We open-source our code at https://github.com/pzy2000/State_Portal and website at https://stateportal.mineyosemite.chatgpt.site
evidence_items.title: StatePortal: Agentic Checkpoint Synthesis for Testing Deep States in Interactive Software

evidence_items.summary: LLM-enhanced recommender systems encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but these embeddings may leak sensitive textual attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, often disrupting the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation. To address it, we introduce relational fidelity as the key objective, requiring semantic shift for privacy while preserving relative item relations for utility. Based on this principle, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO), which learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph. PGPO is optimized with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards. Experiments on two benchmarks show strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance. The code is available at https://github.com/Shengxiang-Lin/PGPO.
evidence_items.title: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
